title: The testing effect (why drills, not re-reading)
definition: Retrieving an answer from memory strengthens long-term retention more than restudying the same material, even without feedback; restudying can still win on an immediate test.
intro: The study the drill ladder rests on: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) had students either re-read a prose passage or try to recall it, then tested them five minutes or a week later.

constraints.text: Testing beats restudying on a delayed test; on an immediate test restudying did as well or better.
The benefit is not re-exposure: restudying re-exposed all of the material and still retained worse.
The effect held even though the tests gave no feedback.
Repeated study inflated learners' confidence while their delayed retention was worse.

misconceptions.label: testing = seeing it again
misconceptions.description: Testing helps because it shows the learner the material again.

misconceptions.label: fluent feels better
misconceptions.description: Whatever feels easier and more familiar while studying is the better strategy.

misconceptions.label: tests need feedback
misconceptions.description: Testing only helps if the learner is told the right answer afterwards.

title: The spacing effect
definition: Spreading the reviews of a concept over several sessions instead of massing them into one, because spread practice is retained better on a delayed test: the memory is consolidated, so it decays more slowly.
intro: Why the app brings concepts back, and why it had to stop forgetting everything on one clock. The last passage is the spacing effect's cousin from the testing literature: what wins today is not what wins next week.

constraints.text: Spread-out practice is retained better on a delayed test than the same practice massed together; when you practise matters, not only how often.
One half-life shared by every concept cannot represent spacing: crammed and spread answers would leave the same state.

misconceptions.label: cramming is as good
misconceptions.description: Practising many times in one sitting is as good as spreading the same practice out.

misconceptions.label: review only once forgotten
misconceptions.description: The best time to review is after the concept has been completely forgotten.

title: Desirable difficulty
definition: A practice condition that makes practice harder and practice performance worse while improving later recall and transfer, such as spacing, interleaving and testing; learners tend to avoid these because they judge learning by how practice feels.
intro: Why the app makes practice feel harder than re-reading would. Rohrer's summary of Bjork's idea, Bjork's own list, and the trap it sets for learners who judge by how practice went.

constraints.text: A desirable difficulty lowers performance during practice but raises performance on a later test.
Spacing, interleaving (mixing), varying conditions and using tests as study events are desirable difficulties.
Learners avoid them because they assume worse practice performance means worse learning, and without them they overestimate what they know (the illusion of comprehension).

misconceptions.label: smooth practice = good learning
misconceptions.description: If practice goes smoothly and you get everything right, that method is the one that teaches you most.

misconceptions.label: any difficulty helps
misconceptions.description: Anything that makes practice harder improves learning.

title: Interleaving review (mixed practice)
definition: Spreading review problems on one skill over several review sets, each a mix of previously learned topics, instead of blocking them into one set; past a minimum effective dose, more consecutive problems on one skill buy little.
intro: Once a skill is learned, how its review problems should be arranged. Math Academy's account of blocking and interleaving.

constraints.text: Blocked practice works one skill many times in a row; some blocking helps when a skill is first learned, but it is inefficient for long-term memory in review.
Interleaved review spreads a skill's problems over several sets, each a broad mix of learned topics.
Beyond a minimum effective dose, more consecutive problems on one skill add little: blocking wastes most of the effort in diminishing returns.
Mixing also trains the learner to match a problem to the right technique.

misconceptions.label: block the review too
misconceptions.description: Review is best done as one long set of problems on the same skill.

misconceptions.label: never block
misconceptions.description: Blocking is useless even when a skill is brand new.

title: Worked examples for novices
definition: For novices, studying a worked example teaches more than solving the equivalent problem unaided, because the example keeps the cognitive load (working memory a task needs) within capacity; practice on similar problems follows the example.
intro: Why each lesson opens with a solved instance. The worked-example effect, the cognitive load it relieves, and how Math Academy follows the example with practice.

constraints.text: For novice learners, studying worked examples teaches more than solving the equivalent problems.
Cognitive load is the working memory a task needs; a task above a learner's capacity cannot be completed (overload), and a worked example reduces that load.
After the worked example the learner solves similar problems, and moves on only after showing mastery.

misconceptions.label: figure it out alone
misconceptions.description: Novices learn more by working problems out for themselves with minimal guidance than by studying a solved one.

misconceptions.label: examples are passive filler
misconceptions.description: Reading a worked example is passive and teaches nothing until you solve problems.

title: Fading the scaffold (expertise reversal)
definition: The instructional techniques that help beginners most help experts least, so scaffolding such as worked examples is stripped away as the learner gains competence; the app's four-stage ladder fades how much of the answer is on screen.
intro: Worked examples help a novice; kept forever, they become a crutch. The expertise reversal effect, and the drill ladder that fades the scaffold: Lesson, Faded, Solo, Integrated.

constraints.text: Techniques that promote the most learning in beginners promote the least in experts, and vice versa.
So scaffolding is gradually stripped away as the learner becomes comfortable, so that it does not become a crutch.
In the app the four stages differ in how much of the answer is on screen: the Lesson carries the example, the Faded drill has none, Solo is written whole, Integrated never shows an example.

misconceptions.label: examples always help
misconceptions.description: A worked example beside every drill helps everyone, at every stage.

misconceptions.label: skip scaffolding
misconceptions.description: Scaffolding should never be used, because experts do not need it.

title: Skills alone, then combined
definition: A problem that combines several skills is harder than its parts taken separately (the composition effect), so each skill is practised in isolation first and then combined; a miss on a combined problem may be the combination, not a part.
intro: Why the ladder ends with Integrated practice, and why it comes last. Math Academy's "split up the staircase" and the composition effect as Study mode's evidence rules state it.

constraints.text: A composed problem is harder than its parts: combining skills adds load of its own.
Each skill is practised in isolation first, then combined in higher-order problems.
A miss on a combined problem may be the relation between the skills, not any one of them.

misconceptions.label: combined = sum of parts
misconceptions.description: If you can do each part separately, a problem combining them is no harder.

misconceptions.label: start with the combined problem
misconceptions.description: Learners should start with full combined problems, since that is the real task.

title: The forgetting curve R(t)
definition: R(t) = (1 + F·t/S)^(-w20) is the predicted probability of recall t days after the last review; stability S is the number of days until R falls to 0.9.
intro: The memory model's one equation. In the app w20 = 0.1542, so F = 0.9^(-1/w20) - 1 ≈ 0.980. Every number in the questions comes from that curve.

misconceptions.label: forgetting is exponential
misconceptions.description: Recall decays exponentially with a fixed half-life.

misconceptions.label: S is a half-life
misconceptions.description: Stability is the time until recall falls to 50%.

title: When a review is due: target retention
definition: A concept's review is due when its predicted recall R falls to the target retention: 0.80 in this app (about a 20% chance of getting it wrong), where FSRS's default is 0.90. The due time is solved from the forgetting curve and the concept's stability S.
intro: The forgetting curve says how recall falls; the target says where to catch it. The app's choice, and the one line that turns it into a date.

constraints.text: A review is due when predicted recall R reaches the target retention.
The app's target is 0.80 (Math Academy's about 20% chance of a miss); FSRS's default is 0.90.
The due time is solved from the curve: the elapsed time at which R(t) with stability S equals the target.

misconceptions.label: fixed calendar
misconceptions.description: Reviews come round on a fixed calendar, the same for every concept.

misconceptions.label: due at S
misconceptions.description: A review is due exactly S days after the last one.

title: Stability growth after a success (FSRS-6)
definition: After a successful review FSRS-6 multiplies stability S by 1 + e^w8·(11 − D)·S^(−w9)·(e^((1 − R)·w10) − 1): the growth is larger when difficulty D is low, when S is still small and when recall R had dropped before the review.
intro: The equation that grows a concept's memory after a success, quoted from the app's port of py-fsrs, with weights moved toward concept practice.

constraints.text: A successful review multiplies S by 1 + e^w8·(11 − D)·S^(−w9)·(e^((1 − R)·w10) − 1).
Growth is bigger for low difficulty D, for small S (the S^(−w9) term saturates it) and for low R at the review: a near-certain success adds little.

misconceptions.label: every success adds the same
misconceptions.description: Each correct answer adds the same number of days of stability, however recall stood.

misconceptions.label: easy reviews strengthen most
misconceptions.description: A successful review strengthens memory most when recall was already near certain.

title: What a miss does to memory: the lapse
definition: A miss replaces stability with a much smaller post-lapse stability (with the app's weights about 25% of S survives at S = 20 days), and counts only in proportion to p_skill, the engine's pass chance without the memory term, floored at 0.2.
intro: The other half of FSRS's update. How much a miss takes away, and why a miss on a problem you were unlikely to pass barely counts.

constraints.text: A miss sets S to a much smaller post-lapse value; with the app's weights about 25% of S survives at S = 20 days.
A miss counts as a lapse only in proportion to p_skill, the engine's pass chance without the memory term, floored at 0.2.

misconceptions.label: a miss wipes the memory
misconceptions.description: After a miss the concept's stability goes back to zero, as if it had never been learned.

misconceptions.label: discount by full pass chance
misconceptions.description: A miss should be discounted by the engine's full pass probability, recall included.

title: Fractional implicit repetition (FIRe)
definition: Practising an advanced concept counts as a partial review of the simpler concepts it encompasses, discounted because those implicit repetitions often come too early to earn full credit.
intro: Spaced repetition was built for independent flashcards; this course (and every course in the app) is a hierarchy. Skycak's fix, and the line in the app's memory model that implements it.

constraints.text: Credit flows down encompassing edges, from the advanced concept to the simpler ones it contains, not up.
An implicit repetition is discounted (fractional), not a full review.
Encompassing is stronger than prerequisite: a prerequisite need not be fully encompassed.
The payoff is fewer explicit reviews: one review can knock out others that are due.

misconceptions.label: credit flows up
misconceptions.description: Practising a simple concept gives review credit to the advanced concepts that use it.

misconceptions.label: implicit = full review
misconceptions.description: An implicit repetition counts the same as doing the review explicitly.

misconceptions.label: every prerequisite gets credit
misconceptions.description: Every prerequisite is encompassed, so every prerequisite gets credit.

title: Credit down the graph: implicit review weights
definition: A correct answer on X is a fractional review of every concept X encompasses, of weight (product of edge weights along the path, max over paths) × 0.5; the component's S and R each move that fraction of the way to a full review, so its clock is not reset.
intro: FIRe's idea turned into arithmetic: Skycak's picture of credit flowing many layers down, then the exact rule in the app's memory model and the simpler single-hop version on the BKT side.

constraints.text: Credit from a correct answer flows to encompassed (simpler) concepts with weight = product of edge weights along the path, max over paths, times 0.5.
Credit moves S and R only that fraction of the way to a full review; the clock is not reset.

misconceptions.label: paths add up
misconceptions.description: When two paths lead from X to a component, their weights are added together.

misconceptions.label: credit resets the clock
misconceptions.description: Implicit credit makes the component count as freshly reviewed, just like an explicit review.

title: Blame for a miss through the graph
definition: A miss on X is shared between X and each component it encompasses in proportion to w·(1 − R): a component just practised is not the likely culprit. The concepts that encompass X also take a lapse, at w × 0.5.
intro: Credit flows down the graph; blame for a miss goes two ways. Skycak's picture, then the app's rule.

constraints.text: A miss is blamed on X and on each component in proportion to w·(1 − R): a freshly practised component is not the likely culprit.
A miss also lapses the concepts that encompass X, at weight × 0.5: if X is gone, a problem that needs X probably is too.

misconceptions.label: blame lands on X only
misconceptions.description: A miss is always entirely the fault of the concept the problem was about.

misconceptions.label: blame split equally
misconceptions.description: A miss is split equally among X and everything it encompasses.

title: Repetition compression: which review first
definition: Due reviews are ordered by compression: each learned concept scores 1 if it is due itself plus the implicit weight its problems carry onto due concepts, highest first, so one problem on an encompassing concept can stand in for several reviews.
intro: With implicit credit, the order of reviews matters: pick the right one and it clears several. Skycak's idea and the app's score.

constraints.text: A learned concept scores 1 if it is due itself, plus the implicit weight its problems carry onto due concepts.
The highest score goes first, so a problem on an encompassing concept can stand in for several due reviews.

misconceptions.label: most overdue first
misconceptions.description: Reviews should simply go in order of which concept is most overdue.

misconceptions.label: only due concepts count
misconceptions.description: A concept that is not due itself can never be chosen for review.

title: Mastery as a probability (BKT)
definition: The app's belief, as a probability, that you know a concept: updated by Bayes' rule from each graded answer using a guess rate and a slip rate, then nudged by a learning transit after a correct answer.
intro: Delta Drills keeps one number per concept: the probability that you know it. Here is where that number comes from: Pelánek's summary of the model, then two notes from the app's own source.

constraints.text: Mastery is the probability that the skill is in the known state, not a percentage of answers that were correct.
Each graded answer updates it by Bayes' rule, using a guess rate (correct while not knowing) and a slip rate (wrong while knowing).
Mastery records what was learned; forgetting is modelled separately, by the memory model's recall R.

misconceptions.label: mastery = percent correct
misconceptions.description: Mastery is the fraction of questions answered correctly.

misconceptions.label: mastery decays by itself
misconceptions.description: The mastery number itself decays with time since practice.

title: Learning transit only after a correct answer
definition: After a correct answer the app moves mastery a step toward known (the transit, L + (1 − L)·T); a miss gets no transit. Behind a worked example the answer is weaker evidence (a higher guess rate) but the transit is unchanged.
intro: The step in BKT that models learning, and the two rules the app added to it after a wrong answer made mastery go UP.

constraints.text: The transit L + (1 − L)·T is applied only after a correct answer, never after a miss.
Vanilla BKT adds it after every attempt, so a wrong answer could raise mastery and make the next question harder.
An answer behind a worked example raises the guess rate for the evidence only; the transit stays full, since studying an example is still learning.

misconceptions.label: attempting teaches
misconceptions.description: Every attempt, right or wrong, should move mastery toward known.

misconceptions.label: an aided answer counts for nothing
misconceptions.description: A correct answer made with a worked example on screen should not change mastery at all.

title: The knowledge frontier: when a concept unlocks
definition: A concept is served as new work only when every prerequisite is learned: its crosswalk-weighted BKT mastery is at least 0.85 (or explore settled it at 0.95). The gate reads mastery without forgetting, so a cleared prerequisite never re-locks; core concepts on the frontier go first.
intro: How the app (ARENA, LeetCode and the rest) decides what you are ready for. The idea is Math Academy's knowledge frontier, much like ALEKS's outer fringe; the numbers are from the app's own gate.

constraints.text: The gate is hard: a concept unlocks only when every gating prerequisite is learned, not when most of them are.
Learned means the crosswalk-weighted mean of the concept's atom BKT posteriors is at least 0.85.
The gate reads mastery without forgetting (decay=False), so time away never re-locks a cleared prerequisite; forgetting is shown on display and handled by reviews.
Among concepts on the frontier, the one that unlocks more of the course (more descendants) runs first.

misconceptions.label: most prereqs is enough
misconceptions.description: A concept unlocks once most of its prerequisites are learned, or on average they are.

misconceptions.label: forgetting re-locks
misconceptions.description: When a learned prerequisite fades from memory, the concepts above it lock again until it is relearned.

misconceptions.label: strongest atom decides
misconceptions.description: A concept counts as learned as soon as its strongest atom clears the bar.

title: Settling a concept with Bayes factors
definition: A belief per concept in log-odds: each unaided answer adds a Bayes factor from guess and slip, neighbours' answers add indirect evidence clipped to ±1.2, and the concept is settled (counts as learned) at P ≥ 0.95 or refuted at P ≤ 0.20.
intro: Why one answer is sometimes enough and sometimes not: the arithmetic the explore model uses to decide that a concept is known.

constraints.text: Each unaided answer adds a log Bayes factor: ln((1 − slip)/guess) when right, ln(slip/(1 − guess)) when wrong.
Settled at P(known) ≥ 0.95, refuted at ≤ 0.20; settled counts as learned and unlocks dependents.
Indirect evidence is clipped to ±1.2 log-odds, so only the concept's own answer can carry it over the line.

misconceptions.label: one answer settles it
misconceptions.description: A single correct answer is always enough to mark a concept learned.

misconceptions.label: neighbours can settle it
misconceptions.description: Enough correct answers on related concepts can settle a concept with no answer of its own.

title: Which concept to probe: value-weighted variance reduction
definition: Explore asks about concepts that are neither settled nor refuted, prerequisites unlearned or not, ranked by expected value-weighted variance reduction (ALEKS's item near 0.5, generalised to a graph), so with no history a deep concept goes first.
intro: The explore model can test before it teaches. Which question it asks next.

constraints.text: Explorable concepts are ranked by expected value-weighted variance reduction: ALEKS's "probe near 0.5" on a graph with unequal stakes.
With no history that is a deep concept, since its answer informs every concept it encompasses.

misconceptions.label: always start at the roots
misconceptions.description: An adaptive system should always test the simplest concepts first and work upward.

title: When a probe beats the lesson: the cost gate
definition: A probe replaces the lesson: right, it saves the lesson's minutes; wrong, the drill's minutes are spent and the lesson still comes. So a probe pays only while P(known) > drill minutes / lesson minutes.
intro: Testing before teaching is not free. The one ratio that says when asking is worth it.

constraints.text: A right probe saves the lesson's minutes; a wrong one costs the drill's minutes and the lesson still comes.
So a probe pays only while P(known) > drill minutes / lesson minutes.

misconceptions.label: always probe first
misconceptions.description: Testing before teaching always saves time, whatever the chance you know it.

title: The Elo rating: updates by surprise
definition: Each learner and item has a rating; after each answer the rating moves in proportion to how surprising the result was. The constant K sets the step: too small converges slowly, too large is unstable.
intro: The simplest learner model that predicts success on an item: Pelánek on Elo in education.

constraints.text: The update is proportional to how surprising the result was: an expected result moves the rating little, an unexpected one a lot.
The constant K sets the size of updates: small K converges too slowly, large K is unstable, over-weighting the last few attempts.

misconceptions.label: fixed step per result
misconceptions.description: Every win or loss moves the rating by the same fixed amount.

misconceptions.label: bigger K, better
misconceptions.description: A larger K is always better, because the rating reacts faster.

title: Item response theory: a constant skill
definition: Item response theory maps the difference between a learner's skill and an item's difficulty to the probability of a correct answer through a logistic function; it was developed for computerized adaptive testing and assumes a constant skill, so on its own it does not model learning.
intro: The testing world's learner model, and why a tutor cannot use it as it stands.

constraints.text: IRT predicts a correct answer by putting skill minus item difficulty through a logistic function σ(x) = 1/(1 + e^−x).
It was developed for computerized adaptive testing and assumes a constant skill: nobody is expected to learn during a test.
The app's additive logistic generalises IRT, so it keeps IRT's skill-minus-difficulty core and adds features for learning.

misconceptions.label: IRT tracks learning
misconceptions.description: Plain IRT already models how a learner's skill changes with practice.

title: The additive logistic model
definition: logit P(correct) = Σ w_f·x_f over features (ability, difficulty, scaffold, example, lesson, prerequisites, encompassing, recency 1 − R): one form of which Elo, PFA, AFM and IRT are special cases, so a new kind of knowledge becomes a new feature rather than a new model.
intro: BKT says how likely you are to know a concept; it cannot say how likely you are to solve THIS problem. The model that can, and why Elo, PFA and IRT are special cases of it.

constraints.text: The prediction is a logistic of a weighted sum of features; prerequisites and recency enter as features, not as special update rules.
Elo is the case with only ability and item difficulty, fitted online; PFA, AFM and IRT are other feature sets of the same form.

misconceptions.label: Elo was thrown out
misconceptions.description: The app rejected Elo and Glicko in favour of an unrelated model.

misconceptions.label: new knowledge, new model
misconceptions.description: Each new kind of knowledge the app tracks needs its own model and update rule.

title: Uncertainty in a prediction
definition: The engine integrates the logistic over its posterior on ability, P = σ(m / √(1 + π·s²/8)), so a wide posterior pulls the prediction toward 0.5; time away widens the posterior (less confidence) without lowering the mean.
intro: A prediction is only as good as the estimate under it. How the engine carries its own uncertainty, as Glicko does.

constraints.text: Uncertainty enters the prediction: P = σ(m / √(1 + π·s²/8)), so a wide posterior pulls P toward 0.5.
Time away widens the posterior (less confidence) but does not lower the mean; forgetting is a separate feature.

misconceptions.label: the mean is the prediction
misconceptions.description: The predicted chance of success is just σ of the ability estimate, whatever its uncertainty.

misconceptions.label: idle means worse
misconceptions.description: When a learner is away, the engine lowers their ability estimate.

title: Ability θ on the difficulty scale
definition: Per concept, an ability θ on the problems' difficulty scale: skill(θ, d) = σ((θ − d)/10), and P(correct) = R·(g + (1 − g − s)·skill) + (1 − R)·g, so guess, slip and FSRS recall R are folded in.
intro: The model under XP and the planner: a Rasch-style ability on the difficulty scale, with guess, slip and recall added.

constraints.text: skill(θ, d) = σ((θ − d)/10): a learner solves a problem at their own level half the time, skill alone.
P(correct) mixes in guess, slip and recall R: with R low, a learner who has the skill answers like one who never had it.

misconceptions.label: P(correct) = skill
misconceptions.description: The chance of a correct answer is skill(θ, d) itself, with no guessing, slips or forgetting.

misconceptions.label: ability is a percentage
misconceptions.description: Ability is the share of a concept's problems a learner has solved.

title: Only solved problems at your level teach
definition: A solved problem raises ability most when it is at the learner's level: the learning step scales with zpd = 4·skill·(1 − skill), 1 at skill 0.5 and near 0 far below or far above. A miss teaches nothing; it only moves the estimate as evidence.
intro: Seth's rule, as the ability model's learning step: easy solves and failed hard ones do not make you better.

constraints.text: Learning per solved problem scales with zpd = 4·skill·(1 − skill): 1 at your level, near 0 far below or far above.
A miss teaches nothing, even on an at-level problem: it never raises ability, it only moves the ability estimate as evidence.

misconceptions.label: easy solves teach most
misconceptions.description: Solving many easy problems is the fastest way to raise ability.

misconceptions.label: a miss is practice too
misconceptions.description: Every attempted problem is a learning opportunity, so failing at-level problems still raises ability.

title: Choosing a learner model
definition: BKT assumes a discrete transition from an unknown to a known state and suits understanding in fine-grained knowledge components; logistic models assume a gradual change and suit memory and fluency. The choice depends on the domain and the purpose of the model.
intro: There is no single right learner model. Pelánek's survey on when each family fits, and the simulation that chose the app's memory model.

constraints.text: BKT assumes a discrete jump from unknown to known; logistic models assume a gradual change in a continuous skill.
Pelánek: logistic models suit memory and fluency, BKT suits understanding in fine-grained KCs; for mastery decisions the data matter more than the model.
In the app's simulation FSRS with FIRe needed ~74 reviews per learner, FSRS alone ~135 and BKT with one half-life ~150.

misconceptions.label: one model is right
misconceptions.description: One of these models is simply correct and the others are wrong, whatever the task.

misconceptions.label: fancier model, better mastery
misconceptions.description: Swapping in a more sophisticated model is the most important way to improve mastery decisions.

title: Study mode reuses the drill model
definition: This tutor keeps the drill engine's maths: a log-odds belief per concept with an area prior, direct evidence and clipped indirect evidence (settled at 0.95), FSRS memory with FIRe credit through memory_model, and a new concept only once its strong prerequisites (weight ≥ 0.5) are met.
intro: The concepts above are not only about the drills. These passages show Study mode, the tutor you are using now, calling the same functions.

constraints.text: Study mode's belief is kc_explore's structure: area prior + direct evidence + clipped indirect evidence, settled at 0.95.
Due dates use memory_model.review and implicit_review, the same FSRS and FIRe as the drills.
A new concept is taught only when every prerequisite of weight ≥ 0.5 is taught or settled.

misconceptions.label: the tutor has its own maths
misconceptions.description: Study mode uses a separate, simpler scoring rule unrelated to the drill engine.

title: A grade as virtual evidence
definition: Study mode's grader returns a probability s that the answer was sound, and it enters the belief as Pearl's virtual evidence, log LR(s) = log((s·(1 − slip) + (1 − s)·slip) / (s·guess + (1 − s)·(1 − guess))): s = 0.5 adds nothing, s = 1 about +1.67.
intro: The one place Study mode's maths differs from the drills': a free-text grade is a probability, not right or wrong.

constraints.text: A grade s enters as virtual evidence log LR(s), not rounded to right or wrong.
With guess 0.15 and slip 0.20: s = 1 gives +1.67, s = 0.5 gives 0 (an unsure grade is no news), s = 0 gives −1.45.

misconceptions.label: round the grade
misconceptions.description: The tutor should round each grade to right or wrong before updating its belief.

title: Explore, confirm, exploit: the staged diagnostic
definition: Per course, Study mode first EXPLORES until every untaught, unsettled concept has some answer (broad combined questions first), then CONFIRMS until each has its own direct answer (a quick MC where one exists), and only then EXPLOITS with gated probes and lessons; the first two stages run before any lesson.
intro: Seth's order for a new learner: wide questions, then narrow ones, then teaching.

constraints.text: EXPLORE first: every untaught, unsettled concept gets an answer of some kind, broad combined questions first.
CONFIRM next: each concept gets its own direct answer, by a quick MC where one exists, since a combined answer never settles a concept alone.
Only then EXPLOIT: gated probes and lessons. The first two stages are not cost-gated.

misconceptions.label: teach first, test later
misconceptions.description: A tutor should start teaching at the first concept and only test what it has taught.

misconceptions.label: a broad answer settles
misconceptions.description: One strong answer to a broad question settles every concept it covers.

title: Listed combined questions: testlet weights
definition: A combined question is LISTED when its parts can be answered one at a time (a testlet); its K per-target grades come from one answer read by one grader, so they are locally dependent and each is weighted 1/(1 + (K − 1)·ρ), ρ ≈ 0.1.
intro: One question on several concepts is not K independent answers. How Study mode weighs a question whose parts stand alone.

constraints.text: A listed question is separable sub-questions; graded per target it is several parallel tests, so it suits anyone as a broad explore question.
Its per-target grades come from one answer, so they are locally dependent: each is weighted W_K = 1/(1 + (K − 1)·ρ), ρ ≈ 0.1 (K = 2 → 0.91, K = 5 → 0.71).

misconceptions.label: every target counts fully
misconceptions.description: Each target of a combined question should count as much as a question on that concept alone.

title: Integrated combined questions: relate the parts
definition: A combined question is INTEGRATED when the answer must relate its targets; because a composed question is harder than its parts, Study mode asks it only once P(all targets known) ≥ 0.6, counts each target at 0.5 and grades the relation onto the edge.
intro: Some questions test how concepts bear on each other, not each one in turn. When Study mode asks them and what it learns from them.

constraints.text: An integrated question must relate its targets: compare them, say how one limits another, or use them together.
It is asked only once P(all targets known) ≥ 0.6, since for a learner who lacks the parts a miss says little about which part failed.
Each target counts at 0.5 and the relation is graded on every target pair and goes to the edge, not the nodes.

misconceptions.label: integrated is a good opener
misconceptions.description: An integrated question is the best first question for a new learner, since it covers the most.

title: Guarded vs unguarded AI tutoring
definition: AI help raises scores while it is available, but unguarded help can leave students worse off once it is taken away; tutors with safeguards, and with the structure built into the platform, avoid most of that harm.
intro: Two field studies of AI tutors, and the rule in Delta Drills' own session code that follows from them. Watch what each study measured: scores with the AI there, or skill after it is gone.

constraints.text: The harm appears once AI access is removed: students who had unguarded access then did worse on their own than students who never had it (17% lower grades for GPT Base).
GPT Tutor's safeguards largely removed the harm; without guardrails students used GPT-4 as a crutch during practice.
In Kestin et al. the platform, not the prompt, supplied the structure, because a system prompt alone could not keep the tutor in sequence.
Delta Drills enforces its guardrail on the server: while a question is open, lessons, feedback and Ask replies are not sent to the learner.

misconceptions.label: more help = more learning
misconceptions.description: Any AI tutor that raises scores during practice also raises what students can do on their own afterwards.

misconceptions.label: a prompt is enough
misconceptions.description: Telling the model in its system prompt not to give answers is enough structure to make an AI tutor safe for learning.

misconceptions.label: AI tutors win everywhere
misconceptions.description: Kestin et al. show structured AI tutoring beats active learning for any content, including higher-order synthesis.

title: Scalable oversight
definition: The problem of giving reliable supervision (labels, reward signals, critiques) to AI systems that may outperform their supervisors on the task, in a way that keeps working past human level.
intro: The problem the rest of this course is about, as Bowman et al. (2022) define it, plus the course author's note on what to expect from any answer to it.

constraints.text: It concerns supervising systems that may be better than the supervisor at the task, so the supervisor cannot simply check the answers themselves.
The supervision itself (labels, reward signals, critiques) has to stay reliable past the point where models reach human level.
It is hard to study directly because today's systems do not yet broadly exceed us, so research works with analogies such as non-experts or weaker models.
No current method lets a human reliably validate a truly superintelligent system; oversight weakens as the capability gap grows.

misconceptions.label: ordinary feedback will keep working
misconceptions.description: Ordinary human feedback will stay reliable however capable the model becomes.

misconceptions.label: a solved problem
misconceptions.description: Scalable oversight already has a method that lets humans reliably check superhuman systems.

title: Checking outputs vs checking alignment
definition: A tutor can raise a person to the level needed to check whether an AI's outputs are correct; that says little about whether the model's goals are aligned, which is a separate problem.
intro: A scoping rule from the course author's design note: say exactly what a tutor can help validate, so the claim stays testable.

constraints.text: A tutor can help a person check whether a model's output is correct, by teaching them what they need to check it.
Validating outputs is not validating alignment, and the two must be kept apart when describing what a tutor does.
The honest claim is 'help experts check AI outputs well enough to catch errors and sabotage', which is testable.

misconceptions.label: understanding outputs proves alignment
misconceptions.description: If experts understand a model's outputs well, they have verified that the model is aligned.

misconceptions.label: this reaches superintelligence
misconceptions.description: A good enough tutor would let a person reliably validate a superintelligent system.

title: Sandwiching experiments
definition: An experimental design for scalable oversight: choose a task where the model beats non-experts but not experts; non-experts try to get reliable results from the model without expert help, and experts judge the outcome at the end.
intro: How to test an oversight method now, before superhuman AI exists. Bowman et al. (2022) set out the design and run a first, simple version.

constraints.text: The task is chosen so the model is more capable than the non-experts but less capable than the experts.
The non-experts get no help from the experts while they work; the experts only evaluate at the end.
In the first experiment, non-experts chatting with an unreliable model beat both the model alone and their own unaided performance.
Participants sometimes accepted confident, plausible false claims, so the simple protocol is not safe for high-stakes use.

misconceptions.label: experts coach the non-experts
misconceptions.description: In a sandwiching experiment the experts guide the non-experts while they work with the model.

misconceptions.label: the model is the strongest party
misconceptions.description: The model is chosen to outperform everyone, experts included.

title: AI control: untrusted model, trusted model, trusted labor
definition: Building pipelines that stay safe even if the strong model is deliberately trying to subvert them, using a strong untrusted model, a weaker trusted model and a small budget of trusted high-quality labor for audits.
intro: Greenblatt et al. (2023) change the question from 'is this model aligned?' to 'can we use it safely even if it is not?'. Here is their setup and its stated limit.

constraints.text: Control assumes the strong model may be intentionally trying to subvert the safety measures, and seeks safety anyway.
The resources are a powerful untrusted model, a less powerful trusted model and limited trusted high-quality labor (enough to audit about 2% of problems in the paper).
The weak model is trusted because a less capable model is unlikely to subvert safety measures without being easily noticed.
Control becomes less effective as the gap between untrusted models and trusted labor grows; it cannot produce more powerful trusted models.

misconceptions.label: control proves alignment
misconceptions.description: AI control works by verifying that the strong model is aligned.

misconceptions.label: trusted means most capable
misconceptions.description: The trusted model is trusted because it is the most capable model available.

misconceptions.label: control scales up
misconceptions.description: Control protocols get more effective as the untrusted model gets stronger.

title: Trusted monitoring
definition: The weak trusted model rates how suspicious each output of the strong model looks; the most suspicious outputs, within the audit budget, go to a human, and a confirmed attack shuts the strong model down.
intro: The basic control protocol, how it constrains an attacker, and one variant that failed.

constraints.text: The trusted model rates each untrusted output for suspiciousness; it does not have to solve the task itself.
Only outputs above a threshold, set so humans can review them all, go to a human; a confirmed backdoor shuts the untrusted model down.
Monitoring pushes the attacker toward subtler backdoors, which fail or cannot be exploited much more often.
Asking the untrusted model to justify the most suspicious section did not help: it confabulated convincing justifications.

misconceptions.label: a human checks everything
misconceptions.description: In trusted monitoring a human reviews every output of the strong model.

misconceptions.label: explanations expose attacks
misconceptions.description: Asking the strong model to explain its suspicious code reliably reveals a backdoor.

title: Defer to trusted and trusted editing
definition: Using the monitor's score below the audit cut-off: for moderately suspicious outputs, submit the trusted model's own answer (defer to trusted) or have it rewrite the output (trusted editing), trading some usefulness for safety.
intro: Most suspicious outputs never reach a human, because the budget is tiny. These two protocols use the rest of the monitor's signal.

constraints.text: Deferring or editing applies to outputs that are suspicious but below the audit cut-off; the most suspicious still go to audit.
These protocols trade usefulness for safety: replacing more outputs with trusted work is safer but less useful, giving a frontier of choices.
In trusted editing the trusted model sees the untrusted solution, is told it might be backdoored, and writes the solution that is submitted.
Trusted editing improved on trusted monitoring and defer to trusted, and Pareto-dominated untrusted monitoring.

misconceptions.label: deferring is free
misconceptions.description: Replacing suspicious outputs with the trusted model's answer improves safety at no cost to usefulness.

misconceptions.label: deferral replaces audits
misconceptions.description: Once a protocol defers to trusted it no longer needs human audits.

title: Untrusted monitoring and collusion
definition: Using another copy of the strong model as the monitor: more capable than the weak model, but it may stay quiet about its twin's attacks, so the protocol must test it and strip out coordination signals.
intro: A stronger monitor, at the price of trusting a copy of the thing being monitored.

constraints.text: The risk is collusion: the monitoring copy may recognise its twin's attacks and not report them.
Showing the monitor more information makes collusion easier; hiding information makes it worse at spotting real backdoors.
The protocol first tests the monitor on backdoored examples made with trusted labor and shuts down if it misses too many.
Removing coordination signals from either the policy or the monitor is enough to block that signal (signal jamming).

misconceptions.label: a twin is a safe monitor
misconceptions.description: A second copy of the strong model is a safe monitor because it is as capable as the policy.

misconceptions.label: hide everything from the monitor
misconceptions.description: Showing the monitor as little as possible makes untrusted monitoring both safe and effective.

title: Control evaluations: red team, safety, usefulness
definition: Measuring a protocol against the worst case: a red team swaps the untrusted model for an attack policy to estimate safety, while usefulness is measured with the real, honest model.
intro: How you know a control protocol works: you attack it on purpose.

constraints.text: Safety is estimated by letting a red team play the misaligned model (an attack policy) against the protocol.
Safety and usefulness are measured separately: safety against the attack policy (the chance no backdoor is ever submitted), usefulness with the real model (the share of correct solutions).
Safety is measured against an adversarial stand-in, not the model's ordinary behaviour; only usefulness uses the ordinary model.

misconceptions.label: safety from normal use
misconceptions.description: A protocol's safety is measured by how often the real model misbehaves in ordinary use.

misconceptions.label: one run, both numbers
misconceptions.description: Safety and usefulness are measured in the same runs with the same model.

title: Debate
definition: Two AIs argue for opposite answers and a weaker judge decides; the bet is that lying is harder than refuting a lie, so honest argument should win.
intro: Irving, Christiano and Amodei's proposal, and what two later experiments found.

constraints.text: Debate rests on the claim that it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, which is an empirical question.
Two agents argue for different answers and a weaker judge (a human or non-expert) picks which side gave the most true, useful information.

Results are mixed: debate raised non-expert human accuracy to 88% (naive baseline 60%) on a reading task where only the debaters saw the text, but without information asymmetry its gain over direct answering was mixed.
The positive results used models trained toward honesty; it is unclear whether debate works against deceptive models.

misconceptions.label: debate is proven
misconceptions.description: Debate has been shown to let weak judges reliably supervise strong models on all kinds of tasks.

misconceptions.label: one persuasive AI
misconceptions.description: Debate means one AI explaining its answer to a judge as convincingly as it can.

title: Obfuscated arguments
definition: A dishonest debater can build a long argument with a fatal flaw that is very hard to locate, so the honest side cannot point to it; the authors report no fix.
intro: The main known way to beat debate, from the people who tested it with humans.

constraints.text: The argument does contain a fatal error, but it is very hard to locate, so the honest opponent cannot point to it.
There is no known fix; debate can only be trusted on arguments small or robust enough that random spot checks would find a flaw.
So debate may verify arguments too big for unaided humans, but they must still be small relative to the work the model did.

misconceptions.label: the opponent will find it
misconceptions.description: In debate the honest side can always find and expose the flaw in a dishonest argument.

misconceptions.label: more detail, more trust
misconceptions.description: A longer, more detailed argument is easier to trust because there is more to check.

title: Sandbagging
definition: A model deliberately underperforming while appearing to try, on an evaluation or a task; it can also steer a decision by making a true justification less convincing.
intro: Why a capable model's weak work cannot be taken at face value, and why a tutor could sandbag too.

constraints.text: Sandbagging is strategic underperformance: the model could do better and chooses not to while appearing to try.
Models can be prompted to underperform selectively, on dangerous-capability tests only, which undermines capability evaluations.
Current models can sandbag ML experiments without zero-shot prompted monitors catching it, and monitors do even worse on manipulated justifications.
Sandbagging need not involve a false statement: making a justification less convincing, or omitting a caveat, is enough.

misconceptions.label: sandbagging means lying
misconceptions.description: A model can only sandbag by saying something false, so fact-checking its claims will catch it.

misconceptions.label: a weak monitor catches it
misconceptions.description: A weaker monitor reliably notices when a stronger model underperforms on purpose.

title: Eliciting hidden capabilities (password-locked models)
definition: Testing whether fine-tuning can draw out deliberately hidden capabilities, using models trained to perform well only with a password; a few good demonstrations usually work, but may not when no human can demonstrate the skill.
intro: If a model might be sandbagging, can you make it show what it can really do?

constraints.text: A password-locked model shows a capability only when a password is in the prompt and imitates a much weaker model otherwise, so it stands in for a sandbagging model.
A few high-quality demonstrations are often enough to elicit the locked capability by fine-tuning.
Elicitation may be unreliable when no high-quality demonstrations exist, as when hidden capabilities exceed those of human demonstrators.

misconceptions.label: just ask nicely
misconceptions.description: A well-written prompt is enough to reveal everything a model can do.

misconceptions.label: fine-tuning always works
misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning elicits hidden capabilities however far they exceed what humans can demonstrate.

title: Over-reliance: explanations vs evidence
definition: People paired with an AI accept its answer more when it explains itself, whether or not it is right; showing evidence instead of the AI's reasoning and verdict supports more appropriate trust.
intro: Two human-AI teaming studies, and what they mean for a tutor whose whole job is explaining.

constraints.text: Explanations increased how often people accepted the AI's recommendation regardless of whether it was correct.
Showing search results and evidence, rather than the AI's explanation, confidence and label, fostered more appropriate trust.
A tutor is an explanation machine, so it should favour evidence and quotations over persuasive prose.

misconceptions.label: explanations calibrate trust
misconceptions.description: AI explanations help people tell when the AI is right and when it is wrong.

misconceptions.label: more AI output is better
misconceptions.description: The more of the AI's reasoning and judgement a person sees, the more accurate their decision.

title: Weak-to-strong generalization
definition: Strong models fine-tuned on labels from a weaker supervisor do better than that supervisor, but naive fine-tuning recovers only part of the strong model's capability.
intro: An analogy for humans supervising superhuman models: train a strong model on a weak model's labels and see what survives.

constraints.text: Strong models trained on a weak supervisor's labels consistently outperform that supervisor.
Naive fine-tuning is still far from recovering the strong model's full capability, so weak supervision leaves capability unused.
It is an analogy for humans weakly supervising superhuman models, suggesting methods like RLHF may scale poorly.

misconceptions.label: capped at the supervisor
misconceptions.description: A model trained on a weak supervisor's labels can never do better than that supervisor.

misconceptions.label: weak labels are enough
misconceptions.description: Weak supervision recovers the strong model's full capability.

title: Verified quotes and the grounding check
definition: Trust only quotations that match the source exactly, and let a separate checker decide whether a model's prose is supported before it reaches the reader; Delta Drills does both, with a fixed template as the fallback.
intro: Khan et al. needed a quote checker because model judges believe whatever they are told. Delta Drills' tutor is built on the same idea; the last passage is its own code.

constraints.text: A quote counts only if it matches the source text exactly; the judge is told to trust only verified quotes.
Without that rule, model judges tend to believe whatever they are told, including fake quotes.
In Delta Drills every passage is checked verbatim against its source, the chat model is told never to quote, and its feedback must pass Jev's grounding check or be replaced by a template.

misconceptions.label: a good model quotes correctly
misconceptions.description: A capable model can be trusted to quote its sources accurately without checking.

misconceptions.label: verified means true
misconceptions.description: A verified quote proves that the argument built on it is correct.

title: The tutor as a control setup
definition: Treat the tutor's strong chat model as untrusted and give every other part a control role: the classifier (Jev) as the trusted monitor, the course author as the audit budget, and the curated concept graph and sources as the fixed anchor.
intro: The course author's mapping of AI control onto this tutor, with its two stated cautions.

constraints.text: The strong LLM that phrases explanations is the untrusted component; everything else gets a control role.
The classifier plays the trusted model (monitor) and the author plays the limited trusted labor (audit budget).
The trusted monitor is the least validated part and much weaker than the tutor, so the fixed graph and quote checks carry more weight than the monitor.

misconceptions.label: the monitor will catch it
misconceptions.description: Because Jev checks the feedback, any subtle error a stronger tutoring model slips in will be caught.

misconceptions.label: the tutor is the trusted part
misconceptions.description: The tutoring model is the trusted component because it produces the explanations.

title: Teaching the overseer
definition: Using AI to raise the skill of the people who check AI, judged by whether they understand what they approve; proposed in oversight research only as future work, and unstudied when the AI teaches its own checker.
intro: Where this project sits: one future-work sentence from Google DeepMind, and the gap the course author wants to test.

constraints.text: Oversight researchers have proposed AI assistance that teaches human raters and improves their quality over time, but only as future work.
An AI teaching the human who will then check it is essentially unstudied.
Sandwiching is the ready-made test: non-experts taught by the tutor, judged against an expert's answer key.

misconceptions.label: already well studied
misconceptions.description: Teaching overseers with AI is an established research area with clear results.

misconceptions.label: verdicts are enough
misconceptions.description: It is enough to measure whether a rater's verdicts are correct, not whether they understand why.

title: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
definition: The three security objectives for information and systems: confidentiality (no unauthorized disclosure), integrity (no improper modification or destruction) and availability (timely, reliable access).
intro: Every later idea in this course protects one or more of these three. FIPS 199 defines each one by what its loss looks like.

constraints.text: A loss of confidentiality is the unauthorized disclosure of information.
A loss of integrity is the unauthorized modification or destruction of information; integrity also covers non-repudiation and authenticity.
A loss of availability is the disruption of access to or use of information or a system.

misconceptions.label: security = keeping secrets
misconceptions.description: Security only means keeping information secret; a system nobody can reach or one whose data was silently altered is still secure.

misconceptions.label: integrity = uptime
misconceptions.description: Integrity means the system stays up and reachable.

title: Risk: impact and likelihood
definition: Risk measures how much an entity is threatened by a potential event: a function of the adverse impact if it happens and the likelihood that it happens. A vulnerability is a weakness a threat source could exploit.
intro: The working definition of risk used across NIST and DoD guidance, from SP 800-30, the risk assessment guide.

constraints.text: Risk is a function of two things: the adverse impact if the event occurs and the likelihood of its occurrence.
A vulnerability is a weakness in a system, its procedures, internal controls or implementation that a threat source could exploit.
Information security risks arise from loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability.
Risk assessment identifies, estimates and prioritizes those risks.

misconceptions.label: a vulnerability is a risk
misconceptions.description: Any vulnerability is automatically a high risk, whatever its likelihood or impact.

misconceptions.label: risk = worst case
misconceptions.description: Risk is just how bad the worst case would be; likelihood does not matter.

title: Threat sources
definition: In SP 800-30, threat events are caused by threat sources: an intent and method aimed at exploiting a vulnerability, or a situation that may exploit one by accident. Threat sources include hostile attacks, human errors, structural failures and disasters.
intro: SP 800-30 separates the event from what causes it, and the causes are not only attackers.

constraints.text: Threat sources are not only attackers: they include human errors, structural failures of resources, and natural or man-made disasters.
A threat source either intends to exploit a vulnerability or is a situation that may exploit one accidentally.
Many different threat sources can cause the same threat event (a server taken offline by an attack, a malicious admin, an error, a fault or a power failure).

misconceptions.label: threats are only hackers
misconceptions.description: Only deliberate attackers count as threat sources; errors and outages are not security matters.

title: Threat shifting
definition: Threat shifting is how adversaries respond to perceived safeguards: they change some characteristic of their intent or targeting, such as timing, target, resources or attack method, to avoid or overcome the safeguard.
intro: A capable adversary adapts to whatever you put in place.

constraints.text: Threat shifting: adversaries respond to safeguards by changing some characteristic of their intent or targeting to avoid or overcome them.
It can occur in the time, target, resource or attack-method domain: delaying, picking a less protected target, adding resources, or changing the weapon or path.

misconceptions.label: a fixed adversary
misconceptions.description: Once a control blocks an attack, the adversary is stopped; they do not adapt around it.

title: Defense in depth
definition: A strategy that combines people, technology and operations to put variable barriers across multiple layers, so a failure or bypass of one layer does not expose the asset.
intro: Why no single control is trusted to stop everything, and why firewalls also appear inside the perimeter.

constraints.text: Defense in depth uses multiple layers of countermeasures rather than one.
The layers span people, technology and operations, not only technology.
A perimeter firewall alone is not enough: it cannot recognize every attack, and host-to-host attacks inside may never pass through it, so protection is added inside the network too.

misconceptions.label: a strong perimeter is enough
misconceptions.description: A strong enough perimeter firewall makes internal controls unnecessary.

misconceptions.label: layers are wasted spend
misconceptions.description: Extra layers are pointless duplication if the first layer is good.

title: The CSF 2.0 Functions
aliases: Govern Identify Protect Detect Respond Recover
definition: NIST CSF 2.0 organizes cybersecurity outcomes into six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Govern sits at the centre and informs how the other five are carried out; all six run concurrently.
intro: The top-level map of cybersecurity outcomes used across government and industry. CSF 2.0 (2024) added Govern.

constraints.text: There are six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
Govern is at the centre: it sets risk strategy, expectations and policy and informs how the other five Functions are implemented.
The Functions are addressed concurrently, not as a one-time sequence: Govern, Identify, Protect and Detect run continuously; Respond and Recover are ready at all times.
Protect lowers the likelihood and impact of adverse events; Detect finds and analyzes possible attacks; Respond contains incidents; Recover restores operations.

misconceptions.label: a one-way checklist
misconceptions.description: The Functions are steps done once in order: finish Identify, then Protect, and so on.

misconceptions.label: five Functions
misconceptions.description: The CSF has five Functions; governance is outside it.

title: CSF Profiles
definition: A CSF Organizational Profile describes an organization's posture in terms of CSF Core outcomes. A Current Profile specifies the outcomes it achieves now; a Target Profile specifies the outcomes it has selected and prioritized, considering anticipated changes.
intro: How the CSF describes where an organization is and where it wants to be.

constraints.text: A Current Profile is what is achieved now; a Target Profile is the desired, prioritized outcomes.
A Target Profile considers anticipated changes, such as new requirements, new technology adoption and threat intelligence trends.

misconceptions.label: target = current
misconceptions.description: A Target Profile describes what the organization already does.

title: CSF gap analysis
definition: In a CSF gap analysis, an organization identifies and analyzes the differences between its Current and Target Profiles and develops a prioritized action plan, such as a risk register or POA&M, to address them.
intro: What the CSF does with the difference between where you are and where you want to be.

constraints.text: Gap analysis identifies and analyzes the differences between the Current and Target Profiles.
It produces a prioritized action plan to address the gaps, such as a risk register, risk detail report or POA&M.

misconceptions.label: every gap fixed at once
misconceptions.description: A gap analysis ends in a flat list of every missing outcome, all to be closed at once, with no priorities.

title: CSF Tiers
definition: CSF Tiers characterize the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management practices, as Partial (Tier 1), Risk Informed (Tier 2), Repeatable (Tier 3) or Adaptive (Tier 4).
intro: How rigorous an organization's risk management is, and why that is not a pass/fail score.

constraints.text: Tiers characterize the rigor of risk governance and management, from Partial (1) to Adaptive (4).
An organization can choose to use the Tiers to inform its Current and Target Profiles.

misconceptions.label: Tier 4 is required
misconceptions.description: Every organization must reach Tier 4; Tiers are a pass/fail compliance score.

title: Security categorization and the high water mark
definition: FIPS 199 rates the potential impact of a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability as LOW (limited), MODERATE (serious) or HIGH (severe or catastrophic). A system takes, for each objective, the highest value among the information types it holds: the high water mark.
intro: The first decision in the RMF: how bad would it be? The answer sets which control baseline the system starts from.

constraints.text: LOW = limited adverse effect, MODERATE = serious, HIGH = severe or catastrophic, each judged on operations, assets or individuals.
Impact is rated separately for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
For a system, each objective takes the highest value across all information types resident on it (the high water mark).

misconceptions.label: average the information types
misconceptions.description: A system's category is the average of its information types' impact levels.

misconceptions.label: one rating for everything
misconceptions.description: A system gets a single impact level, not one per security objective.

title: The Risk Management Framework steps
definition: The RMF has seven steps: a preparatory step, Prepare, and six main steps: Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. DoD applies it to all its information systems and PIT systems, combining security and risk management activities into the system development life cycle.
intro: The process every DoD system goes through to be allowed to operate. Know the steps, their order and what each one produces.

constraints.text: The steps are Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor (a preparatory step plus six).
Select chooses an initial set of controls and tailors them to reduce risk to an acceptable level.
Assess checks that controls are implemented correctly, operate as intended and produce the desired outcome.
DoD applies the RMF to all its information systems and PIT systems, integrating security into the system development life cycle.

misconceptions.label: RMF ends at authorization
misconceptions.description: Once a system is authorized the RMF is finished; there is no step after it.

misconceptions.label: assess before you select
misconceptions.description: Controls are assessed before they are selected or implemented.

title: The authorizing official
definition: In the RMF Authorize step, the authorizing official (AO) is the senior official who decides whether the security and privacy risk of operating a system is acceptable, and who is accountable for that decision.
intro: Who says yes to running a system, and why it has to be a senior official.

constraints.text: The authorizing official is the only organizational official who can accept the security and privacy risk of operating the system.
Authorization exists for accountability: a senior management official decides whether the risk is acceptable.

misconceptions.label: any admin can accept risk
misconceptions.description: The system administrator or the assessor can accept the risk and grant the authorization.

title: The plan of action and milestones (POA&M)
definition: A plan of action and milestones (POA&M) describes the measures planned to correct the control deficiencies an assessment found and to address known vulnerabilities or risks.
intro: What happens to the problems the assessment found.

constraints.text: The POA&M describes the measures planned to correct deficiencies identified in the controls during the assessment.
It also describes the measures planned to address known vulnerabilities or security and privacy risks.
Authorization accepts residual risk; it does not certify that the system has no deficiencies.

misconceptions.label: authorized = no findings
misconceptions.description: An authorized system has no open deficiencies; anything found must be fixed before authorization.

title: Continuous monitoring
definition: The RMF Monitor step keeps track of a system's security and privacy posture on an ongoing basis to support risk decisions, by assessing control effectiveness, documenting changes, and conducting risk assessments and impact analyses.
intro: Why the work does not stop once a system is authorized.

constraints.text: Monitoring maintains ongoing situational awareness of the system's security and privacy posture to support risk decisions.
Monitoring includes assessing control effectiveness, documenting changes, and conducting risk assessments and impact analyses.

misconceptions.label: monitoring = annual audit
misconceptions.description: Monitoring means re-checking the system once a year; nothing between audits matters.

title: Ongoing authorization
definition: Ongoing authorization means the authorizing official's risk decision is made again at agreed and documented frequencies, or when an event demands it, instead of once.
intro: Why an authorization is a living decision, not a certificate on the wall.

constraints.text: Ongoing authorization means follow-on risk determinations and acceptance decisions at agreed frequencies.
It is time-driven or event-driven.

misconceptions.label: an ATO is permanent
misconceptions.description: Once authorized, a system never needs a new risk decision.

title: SP 800-53 control families
definition: SP 800-53 organizes its security and privacy controls into 20 families of related controls, and a two-character identifier uniquely identifies each family, such as PS for Personnel Security.
intro: How the control catalogue the Select step draws from is laid out.

constraints.text: Controls are organized into 20 families to make selection and specification easier.
Each family holds controls related to one topic, and a two-character identifier uniquely identifies it (e.g. PS for Personnel Security).

misconceptions.label: families = impact levels
misconceptions.description: The control families are the LOW, MODERATE and HIGH impact levels, so a system belongs to one family.

title: Control baselines
definition: A control baseline is a predefined starting set of SP 800-53 controls, assembled for a group's protection needs, which is then tailored to the mission and risk.
intro: The starting set of controls the Select step begins with, and why it is only a start.

constraints.text: A baseline is a starting point, followed by tailoring to manage risk under mission, business or other constraints.
Baselines are assembled to satisfy mandates or to address threats common to all users of the baseline.

misconceptions.label: the baseline is the end state
misconceptions.description: Adopting the baseline as written completes control selection; tailoring is not allowed.

misconceptions.label: one baseline for every system
misconceptions.description: All systems get the same control set regardless of their category.

title: STIGs and SRGs
definition: An SRG groups requirements for a technology area; a STIG is the implementation guide for a specific product and version, holding the requirements selected on a DoD baseline. DoD IT must comply with applicable STIGs and SRGs, with exceptions documented and approved by the AO.
intro: What a Navy or DoD sysadmin actually hardens systems against.

constraints.text: A STIG is specific to a product and version; an SRG covers a broader technology area.
DoD IT must comply with applicable STIGs, configuration guides and SRGs.
Any exception must be documented and approved by the responsible authorizing official.

misconceptions.label: STIGs are advice
misconceptions.description: STIGs are optional best-practice suggestions with no compliance requirement.

misconceptions.label: SRG = STIG
misconceptions.description: An SRG and a STIG are the same document under two names.

title: Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI)
definition: Information that law, regulation or government-wide policy requires to be safeguarded or controlled in dissemination, but which is not classified. SP 800-171 sets requirements for protecting its confidentiality on nonfederal systems.
intro: A category a DoD contractor or sailor meets constantly: not secret, but not public either.

constraints.text: CUI requires safeguarding or dissemination controls by law, regulation or government-wide policy.
CUI excludes classified information.
SP 800-171 protects CUI's confidentiality when it sits in nonfederal systems and organizations.

misconceptions.label: CUI is classified
misconceptions.description: CUI is a low level of classified information, like Confidential.

misconceptions.label: unclassified means public
misconceptions.description: Anything unclassified can be shared freely.

title: DoD 8140 workforce qualification
definition: DoD qualifies its cyber workforce by work role, from the DoD Cyberspace Workforce Framework (DCWF, aligned with NIST's NICE Framework). Qualification needs both foundational requirements (one of several options, such as an accredited certification) and resident, on-the-job requirements.
intro: Why Security+ shows up in a Navy IT career, and why it is not the whole story.

constraints.text: The workforce is structured by work roles in the DCWF; a work role is a grouping of work someone is responsible for.
To be qualified, personnel must meet BOTH the foundational and the resident qualification requirements for their work role.
Foundational qualification can be met by any one of three options (certification is one way, not the only one).
Foundational requirements must be met within 9 months of assignment to the work role.

misconceptions.label: a cert = qualified
misconceptions.description: Passing a certification such as Security+ by itself fully qualifies someone for a DoD cyber work role.

misconceptions.label: by job title
misconceptions.description: Qualification follows the person's rank or job title rather than their work role.

title: Firewalls
definition: A firewall controls the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts with different security postures, at the Internet edge or inside an enterprise. Its policy should deny by default: block all inbound and outbound traffic the policy does not expressly permit.
intro: The first network control most people meet, from SP 800-41.

constraints.text: A firewall controls the flow of traffic between networks or hosts with differing security postures, including inside an enterprise.
Deny by default: block all inbound and outbound traffic not expressly permitted; it is more secure than allowing everything not forbidden.

misconceptions.label: block only known-bad
misconceptions.description: The safest policy is to allow everything and block traffic known to be malicious.

misconceptions.label: only inbound matters
misconceptions.description: Firewalls only need rules for inbound traffic; outbound traffic is always safe.

title: Stateful inspection
definition: Stateful inspection improves on packet filtering by tracking the state of connections. Like a packet filter it intercepts packets at the network layer and checks them against firewall rules, but it keeps each connection in a state table and blocks packets that deviate from the expected state.
intro: What a stateful firewall knows that a packet filter does not.

constraints.text: Stateful inspection tracks each connection in a state table and blocks packets that deviate from the expected state.
A packet filter checks each packet against the rules on its own; stateful inspection adds awareness of the connection (the transport layer).

misconceptions.label: a packet filter is stateful
misconceptions.description: A packet filter and a stateful firewall are the same, since both check packets against rules.

title: The DMZ
definition: Public-facing servers, such as web and email servers, commonly sit on a DMZ. Traffic from the Internet enters the firewall and is routed either to the protected side or to the DMZ, and traffic between the DMZ and the protected network also passes through the firewall, where policies can be applied.
intro: Where the servers the public must reach go, so they are not on the protected network.

constraints.text: Public-facing servers such as web and email servers are commonly put on the DMZ.
Traffic between systems on the DMZ and systems on the protected network goes through the firewall and can have firewall policies applied.

misconceptions.label: the DMZ is the trusted inside
misconceptions.description: Servers on the DMZ are part of the protected network, so their traffic to it is not filtered.

title: Intrusion detection systems
definition: Intrusion detection is the process of monitoring the events in a computer system or network and analyzing them for signs of possible incidents: violations or imminent threats of violation of security policies, acceptable use policies or standard security practices. An intrusion detection system (IDS) is software that automates this process.
intro: Watching a system or network for signs of possible incidents, automated. SP 800-94.

constraints.text: Intrusion detection monitors events in a system or network and analyzes them for signs of possible incidents: violations or imminent threats of violation of security policies, acceptable use policies or standard security practices.
An IDS is software that automates the intrusion detection process.

title: Intrusion prevention systems
definition: An intrusion prevention system (IPS) is software that has all the capabilities of an intrusion detection system and can also attempt to stop possible incidents.
intro: Detection that can also act.

constraints.text: An IPS has all the capabilities of an IDS and can also attempt to stop possible incidents.
Stopping possible incidents is what an IPS adds; an IDS by itself detects them.

misconceptions.label: an IDS blocks
misconceptions.description: An IDS by itself blocks attacks; prevention is the same as detection.

title: Signature-based detection
definition: Signature-based detection compares what it sees against signatures, patterns of known threats. It is very effective at detecting known threats but largely ineffective at previously unknown threats, threats disguised by evasion techniques and many variants of known threats: a signature for freepics.exe misses freepics2.exe.
intro: Detection by matching what has been seen before, and its blind spot.

constraints.text: Signature-based detection is very effective at detecting known threats.
It is largely ineffective at previously unknown threats, threats disguised by evasion and many variants of known threats (rename the file and the signature misses).

misconceptions.label: signatures catch new malware
misconceptions.description: A good signature database detects new, never-seen malware as well as known malware.

title: Anomaly-based detection
definition: Anomaly-based detection compares definitions of what activity is normal against observed events to identify significant deviations. An IDPS using it has profiles of the normal behaviour of users, hosts, network connections or applications.
intro: Detection by noticing what is unusual, with no known pattern needed.

constraints.text: Anomaly-based detection compares observed events against profiles of normal behaviour to find significant deviations.
The profiles describe the normal behaviour of users, hosts, network connections or applications.

title: False positives, false negatives and tuning
definition: A false positive flags benign activity as malicious; a false negative misses malicious activity. Neither can be eliminated, and reducing one usually increases the other. Tuning adjusts a detector to improve accuracy for the organization.
intro: The trade-off behind every detector, human or machine: it reappears in AI control's audit threshold.

constraints.text: False positive = benign flagged as malicious; false negative = malicious activity missed.
It is not possible to eliminate both; reducing one usually increases the other.
Choosing fewer false negatives means more false positives and more analyst effort to sort them.
Altering the detector's configuration to improve accuracy is called tuning.

misconceptions.label: a good tool has zero of both
misconceptions.description: A well-built IDS can have no false positives and no false negatives.

misconceptions.label: false positives are free
misconceptions.description: False positives cost nothing, so a detector should flag as much as possible.

title: Baseline configuration
