definition: A baseline configuration is a set of specifications for a system, or a configuration item within it, that has been formally reviewed and agreed at a given point in time and can be changed only through change control procedures. It is the basis for future builds, releases and changes.
intro: The agreed record every later change is measured against. SP 800-128.

constraints.text: A baseline configuration is formally reviewed and agreed at a point in time and can be changed only through change control procedures.
The baseline is the basis for future builds, releases and changes.

misconceptions.label: a baseline is just a backup
misconceptions.description: A baseline configuration is a backup image that anyone may update directly.

title: Configuration change control
definition: Configuration change control is the documented process for managing and controlling changes to a system's configuration or its configuration items: the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, test/evaluation, review and disposition of changes, including upgrades and modifications.
intro: How a hardened system stays hardened. SP 800-128.

constraints.text: Change control is a documented process: proposal, justification, implementation, test/evaluation, review and disposition of changes.
It covers every change to the system's configuration, including upgrades and modifications.

misconceptions.label: small changes skip control
misconceptions.description: Small or urgent changes can be made directly without going through change control.

title: Patching as a cost of doing business
definition: SP 800-40r4 says patching should be considered a standard cost of doing business, rigorously followed and tracked, like preventive maintenance on fleet vehicles: an organization that needs a technology for its mission must maintain it throughout its life cycle, and that includes patching.
intro: SP 800-40r4 reframes patching as maintenance, not emergency work.

constraints.text: Patching is a normal, necessary cost of using technology through its life cycle, and should be rigorously followed and tracked.
An organization that needs a technology for its mission must maintain it throughout its life cycle, and that includes patching.

misconceptions.label: patching is optional extra work
misconceptions.description: Patching is extra work done only after an incident.

title: Risk responses for vulnerable software
definition: For vulnerable software an organization chooses a risk response. Accept: rely on existing controls or judge the impact low enough. Mitigate: eliminate the vulnerability (patch, disable the feature, upgrade) and/or add controls such as firewalls and segmentation that isolate the asset. Transfer: share consequences with another party, such as an insurer or a SaaS provider that patches.
intro: SP 800-40r4's answer when the question is not just 'is there a patch?'.

constraints.text: Risk responses include accepting, mitigating and transferring the risk; patching is one form of mitigation.
Mitigation can also mean isolating vulnerable assets with firewalls and segmentation when a patch is not possible.

misconceptions.label: patch or nothing
misconceptions.description: The only acceptable response to a vulnerability is to install a patch.

title: Zero trust
definition: Zero trust grants no implicit trust based on network location or asset ownership. Authentication and authorization of subject and device happen before each session to a resource; assets act as if an attacker is already on the network, authenticating connections and encrypting traffic.
intro: The move from 'inside the firewall = trusted' to 'verify every session'. It is also NIST's first tip against ransomware.

constraints.text: No implicit trust is granted because of network location (inside the LAN) or because an asset is enterprise-owned.
Authentication and authorization of both subject and device are performed before a session to a resource is established.
Assets act as if an attacker is present on the network: authenticate all connections and encrypt all traffic.
Segmenting internal networks limits how far malware can spread.

misconceptions.label: inside the VPN = trusted
misconceptions.description: Once a user is on the internal network or VPN, their traffic can be trusted.

misconceptions.label: zero trust is a product
misconceptions.description: Zero trust is a single product you buy, not a set of principles.

title: Authentication factors and MFA
definition: The three authentication factors are something you know, something you have and something you are. Multi-factor authentication requires more than one DISTINCT type of factor.
intro: SP 800-63B, NIST's authentication guideline: what counts as a second factor and what does not.

constraints.text: The three factor types are something you know, something you have and something you are.
MFA requires more than one distinct TYPE of factor; two of the same type is not multi-factor.

misconceptions.label: two passwords = MFA
misconceptions.description: Asking for a password and then a security question is multi-factor authentication.

misconceptions.label: MFA stops all phishing
misconceptions.description: Any MFA method makes phishing impossible.

title: Phishing-resistant authentication
definition: Phishing resistance is an authentication protocol's ability to keep secrets and authenticator outputs from an impostor verifier without relying on the user's vigilance. It requires cryptographic authentication; manually typed codes (OTP, out-of-band) are not phishing-resistant because they are not bound to the session.
intro: Why a one-time code can be phished and a security key cannot.

constraints.text: Phishing resistance protects authentication secrets from an impostor verifier WITHOUT relying on the claimant's vigilance.
It requires single- or multi-factor cryptographic authentication.
Manually entered outputs such as OTP and out-of-band codes are not phishing-resistant: they are not bound to the session, so an impostor can relay them.

misconceptions.label: codes are phishing-proof
misconceptions.description: A one-time code sent by text or app is phishing-resistant because it expires quickly.

misconceptions.label: training = resistance
misconceptions.description: Training users to spot fake sites makes any authenticator phishing-resistant.

title: Least privilege
definition: Allow only the accesses that users, and processes acting for them, need for their assigned tasks, and run processes at no higher privilege than necessary. Admins use non-privileged accounts for non-security work.
intro: SP 800-53 control AC-6, the control behind 'don't browse the web as admin' and, later, 'don't give the AI agent write access'.

constraints.text: Only the accesses necessary to accomplish assigned tasks are allowed, for users and for processes acting on their behalf.
It applies to system processes too: they run at privilege levels no higher than necessary.
Using non-privileged accounts for non-security functions limits exposure from privileged accounts.

misconceptions.label: trusted people get full access
misconceptions.description: Trusted senior staff should have full access everywhere to avoid slowing them down.

misconceptions.label: only people
misconceptions.description: Least privilege applies to human users, not to software processes.

title: Separation of duties
definition: Split mission and support functions among different people or roles so that abusing authorized privilege requires collusion; for example, the people who administer access control do not also administer audit.
intro: SP 800-53 AC-5: no single person both does the thing and checks the thing.

constraints.text: It reduces the risk of malevolent activity because abuse would need collusion between people.
Functions are divided among different individuals or roles.
Security staff who administer access control do not also administer audit functions.

misconceptions.label: one admin for efficiency
misconceptions.description: Having the same administrator manage both access and the audit logs is fine if they are trusted.

misconceptions.label: same as least privilege
misconceptions.description: Separation of duties is just another name for least privilege.

title: ATT&CK tactics and techniques
definition: In MITRE ATT&CK, tactics are the 'why': the adversary's tactical goal, the reason for performing an action, such as Initial Access or Privilege Escalation. Techniques are the 'how': the action by which the adversary achieves a tactical goal. SP 800-30 characterizes threat events by the adversary's tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).
intro: A shared vocabulary for describing what attackers do, used to plan detections and assess coverage.

constraints.text: A tactic is the 'why': the adversary's tactical goal, the reason for performing an action.
A technique is the 'how': a way of achieving a tactic (Phishing is a technique for Initial Access).
Threat events are characterized by the adversary's tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).
Tactics include Initial Access (getting into the network), Execution, Persistence and Privilege Escalation.

misconceptions.label: tactic = how
misconceptions.description: A tactic is the specific method an attacker uses; a technique is their goal.

misconceptions.label: a fixed kill chain
misconceptions.description: Every attack must pass through every tactic in a fixed order.

title: Social engineering
definition: Social engineering is a technique that relies heavily on human interaction to influence a person to violate security protocol or divulge confidential information, commonly by phone or online.
intro: Attacking the people instead of the machines.

constraints.text: Social engineering relies on human interaction to influence someone to violate security protocol or divulge information.
It is commonly committed by phone or online; for example, an attacker posing as an existing customer to get a company to divulge information about that customer.

misconceptions.label: only a system flaw counts
misconceptions.description: An attack must exploit a technical flaw in a system; persuading a person to hand something over is not an attack.

misconceptions.label: social engineering = email
misconceptions.description: Social engineering only happens by email; a phone call asking for information is not an attack.

title: Phishing
definition: Phishing is electronically delivered social engineering, either targeted at a specific individual, company or industry (spearphishing) or untargeted, as in mass spam campaigns, often carrying malicious attachments or links.
intro: The most common way in. ATT&CK lists it as technique T1566 under Initial Access.

constraints.text: Phishing is electronically delivered social engineering, either targeted (spearphishing) or non-targeted mass campaigns.
Mitigations include anti-spoofing and email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and training users to recognize phishing.

misconceptions.label: a purely technical attack
misconceptions.description: Phishing is a purely technical exploit; human behaviour has nothing to do with it.

misconceptions.label: filters solve it
misconceptions.description: Email authentication alone stops all phishing, so training is unnecessary.

title: Ransomware
definition: Malware that encrypts an organization's data and demands payment to restore access, and may also steal data and demand payment not to disclose it. Its impact on operations is immediate, so preparation (tested, isolated backups; segmentation) is critical.
intro: NIST IR 8374 frames ransomware as a CSF profile: prepare before it happens.

constraints.text: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment for restoring access; it can also steal data and extort payment for not disclosing it.
Its impact on business operations is immediate, leaving little time to respond, so organizations must be prepared in advance.
Plan, implement and test backup and restoration, and secure and isolate the backups.

misconceptions.label: backups make it harmless
misconceptions.description: Having backups makes ransomware harmless, including the data-theft part.

misconceptions.label: backups need no testing
misconceptions.description: Any backup will restore correctly when needed, so testing restoration is unnecessary.

title: Penetration testing vs vulnerability scanning
definition: Vulnerability scanning identifies outdated software, missing patches and misconfigurations by matching what is running against a database of known vulnerabilities. Penetration testing mimics real-world attacks, often chaining vulnerabilities, to find ways around security features.
intro: Two kinds of security testing from SP 800-115, and what each can tell you.

constraints.text: Scanning matches identified systems and software against known vulnerabilities in the scanner's database, finding missing patches and misconfigurations.
Penetration testing mimics real-world attacks, often with real attacks on real systems, to find ways to circumvent security features.
Pen tests look for combinations of vulnerabilities that give more access than any single one.

misconceptions.label: a scan is a pen test
misconceptions.description: A vulnerability scan and a penetration test are the same activity.

misconceptions.label: scanners find everything
misconceptions.description: A vulnerability scanner can find unknown vulnerabilities as well as known ones.

title: Insider threat
definition: Insiders are dangerous because they know the systems and what would cause the most damage. Insider threat programs detect and prevent malicious insider activity by integrating technical and non-technical information; access is cut immediately when someone leaves.
intro: The threat that already has an account. Keep it in mind for the capstone: an AI agent with access is an insider too.

constraints.text: Insiders are a threat because of their familiarity with the systems and with what actions would cause the most damage.
Insider threat programs combine technical and non-technical information, centrally, to detect and prevent malicious insider activity.
A terminated employee's access should be disabled immediately.

misconceptions.label: threats come from outside
misconceptions.description: With a strong perimeter the organization is safe; people with legitimate access are not a threat.

misconceptions.label: logs alone
misconceptions.description: Insider threats are caught with technical logs alone; non-technical information is irrelevant.

title: Log management
definition: A log is a record of the events in an organization's systems and networks. The fundamental problem of log management is balancing a limited amount of resources against a continuous supply of log data.
intro: Detection runs on data. SP 800-92 on where it comes from and why it is hard.

constraints.text: A log is a record of events; logs now serve investigation of malicious activity, not just troubleshooting.
The fundamental problem is balancing limited log management resources against a continuous, high-volume supply of log data from many sources and formats.
Logs themselves must be protected for confidentiality, integrity and availability.

misconceptions.label: log everything, problem solved
misconceptions.description: Collecting every possible log solves detection; volume is never a problem.

title: SIEM
definition: Security information and event management (SIEM) software is centralized logging software: its log servers analyze the logs from many sources, correlating events and identifying and prioritizing significant ones, and its database servers store them.
intro: The centralized software many security teams analyze their logs in, and what it does and does not do.

constraints.text: A SIEM has log servers that analyze logs and database servers that store them.
A SIEM server analyzes data from all the log sources, correlates events among log entries, identifies and prioritizes significant events, and can initiate automated responses.
SIEM software is usually much more complicated and expensive to deploy than a centralized syslog implementation.

misconceptions.label: the SIEM does the analysis for you
misconceptions.description: Buying a SIEM removes the need for people to analyze logs.

title: Events, adverse events and incidents
definition: An event is any observable occurrence involving computing assets; adverse events have negative consequences. An incident actually or imminently jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or a system, or violates law or security policy. Analysis decides whether adverse events add up to an incident.
intro: SP 800-61r3's vocabulary: not every alert is an incident.

constraints.text: An event is any observable occurrence (a login attempt, a software update).
An incident actually or imminently jeopardizes CIA without lawful authority, or violates (or imminently threatens to violate) law, security policies or acceptable use policies.
Further analysis is often needed to decide whether adverse events indicate an incident.

misconceptions.label: every alert is an incident
misconceptions.description: Every security alert or adverse event is by definition an incident.

misconceptions.label: only after damage
misconceptions.description: Something is only an incident once damage has actually occurred; an imminent threat does not count.

title: Incident response on CSF 2.0
definition: SP 800-61r3 maps incident response onto the CSF 2.0 Functions: Detect, Respond and Recover are incident response itself; Govern, Identify and Protect are broader preparation; lessons learned feed continuous Improvement into every Function, as soon as they are identified.
intro: The 2025 revision replaced the old linear life cycle because incidents are now frequent and damaging.

constraints.text: Detect, Respond and Recover are the incident response activities themselves.
Govern, Identify and Protect are broader risk management activities that prepare for and reduce incidents.
Lessons learned feed continuous improvement into all Functions and should be shared as soon as identified, not held until recovery ends.
The model changed because incidents now occur frequently, cause more damage and can take weeks or months to recover from.

misconceptions.label: lessons at the end
misconceptions.description: Lessons learned are written up only after recovery is complete.

misconceptions.label: IR is its own silo
misconceptions.description: Incident response is a separate activity unconnected to the rest of risk management.

title: Prompt injection
definition: Input that alters an LLM's behaviour or output in unintended ways. In direct prompt injection the user's own input does it, appending instructions that compete with higher-trust instructions such as the system prompt. The input need not be human-readable, and there may be no fool-proof prevention.
intro: OWASP's number-one LLM risk and NIST's name for the attack.

constraints.text: Prompt injection is input that alters the model's behaviour or output in unintended ways.
In direct prompt injection the user's own prompt does it, adding instructions that override higher-trust ones such as the system prompt.
Injected content need not be visible or readable to humans, only parsed by the model.
Because of how generative models work, it is unclear that fool-proof prevention exists; measures mitigate impact.

misconceptions.label: a filter fixes it
misconceptions.description: A good enough input filter or system prompt reliably prevents prompt injection.

misconceptions.label: you can see it
misconceptions.description: A prompt injection is always visible text a human reviewer would notice.

title: Indirect prompt injection
definition: Attackers plant instructions in resources the model reads (web pages, documents, RAG results). Because GenAI combines the data and instruction channels, control of a resource lets an attacker inject instructions without talking to the application, threatening availability, integrity and privacy.
intro: Why an agent that reads the web is a different security problem from a chatbot.

constraints.text: GenAI models combine the data and instruction channels, so data the model reads can act as instructions.
The attacker controls a resource the system interacts with (a site, file or retrieved document) rather than the prompt itself.
It can violate availability, integrity or privacy.
A mitigation is to separate and clearly mark untrusted external content to limit its influence.

misconceptions.label: only the user can inject
misconceptions.description: Only the person typing into the chat can inject instructions.

misconceptions.label: data is just data
misconceptions.description: Content the model retrieves is treated purely as data and cannot change its behaviour.

title: Excessive agency
definition: Damaging actions an LLM-based system can take in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs, whatever made the model misbehave. Root causes are excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy; mitigations are minimal extension permissions and human approval of high-impact actions.
intro: Least privilege, applied to an AI agent's tools.

constraints.text: It is about the damage the system can do regardless of what causes the model to malfunction (hallucination, injection, a compromised agent).
The root causes are excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.
Mitigate by giving extensions the minimum permissions necessary (e.g. read-only access to one table).
Require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken.

misconceptions.label: fix the model, not the permissions
misconceptions.description: Excessive agency is solved by making the model more accurate; its permissions do not matter.

misconceptions.label: only attacks cause it
misconceptions.description: Excessive agency only matters when an attacker injects a prompt.

title: Adversarial ML taxonomy
definition: NIST's taxonomy sorts attacks on ML by stage (training-time poisoning, deployment-time evasion, privacy and availability attacks) and by goal: availability breakdown, integrity violation or privacy compromise.
intro: The map of what can go wrong with a model, from NIST AI 100-2.

constraints.text: Training-time poisoning attacks control part of the training data (data poisoning) or the model and its parameters (model poisoning).
Deployment-time attacks, such as evasion, availability and privacy attacks, are mounted against a deployed model.
Attacker objectives are classified as availability breakdown, integrity violation and privacy compromise, mirroring CIA.
Privacy attacks such as membership inference and data reconstruction need only query access to a deployed model.

misconceptions.label: attacks need training access
misconceptions.description: An attacker must get into the training pipeline to attack a model.

title: Evasion attacks
definition: Evasion attacks are deployment-time attacks that modify testing samples into adversarial examples: inputs similar to the original sample, by certain distance metrics, that alter the model's predictions to the attacker's choices.
intro: Attacking a finished model through its inputs, with no access to its training.

constraints.text: Evasion attacks are mounted against deployed models by modifying testing samples.
An adversarial example is similar to the original sample, by certain distance metrics, but alters the model's prediction to the attacker's choice.

misconceptions.label: adversarial = obviously different
misconceptions.description: Adversarial examples look obviously different from normal inputs.

title: Data poisoning
definition: Data poisoning is the manipulation of pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors or biases. In NIST's taxonomy it is a training-time attack in which the adversary controls a subset of the training data.
intro: OWASP LLM04: attacking a model through the data it learns from.

constraints.text: Poisoning manipulates pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors or biases.
It is a training-time attack: in data poisoning the adversary controls a subset of the training data by inserting or modifying samples; in model poisoning, the model and its parameters.
It can compromise model security, performance or ethical behaviour, leading to harmful outputs or impaired capabilities.

misconceptions.label: only pre-training
misconceptions.description: Only pre-training data can be poisoned; fine-tuning and embeddings are safe.

title: Backdoors
definition: A backdoor, which poisoning may implant, leaves a model's behaviour untouched until a certain trigger causes it to change. Because normal behaviour is unchanged, a backdoor is hard to test for and detect: the model can become a sleeper agent.
intro: Why testing a model's normal behaviour does not prove it safe.

constraints.text: A backdoor leaves behaviour untouched until a certain trigger causes it to change.
Because normal behaviour is unchanged, backdoors are hard to test for and detect, in effect a sleeper agent.

misconceptions.label: normal tests catch it
misconceptions.description: A poisoned model will reveal itself in ordinary accuracy testing.

title: Deploying AI systems securely
definition: AI systems are software systems: prefer secure-by-design systems and apply ordinary security. Model weights are a critical asset (they embody costly compute, data and algorithms), so harden the interfaces to them against exfiltration and return only minimal data from APIs.
intro: The NSA-led guidance for organizations deploying AI they did not build.

constraints.text: AI systems are software systems, so deployers should prefer secure-by-design systems and apply normal security practice.
Model weights are particularly critical to protect because they represent costly compute, sensitive data and algorithmic work.
Harden interfaces to weights to make exfiltration harder; have APIs return only the minimal data needed (to inhibit model inversion).

misconceptions.label: AI needs no ordinary security
misconceptions.description: AI security is entirely new; ordinary software security does not apply to AI systems.

misconceptions.label: weights are not sensitive
misconceptions.description: Model weights are just numbers and need no special protection.

title: The AI Risk Management Framework
definition: NIST's AI RMF organizes AI risk management into four functions: Govern (cross-cutting), Map (establish context and frame risks), Measure (analyze, assess, benchmark and monitor, before and during deployment) and Manage (allocate resources to mapped and measured risks).
intro: The AI counterpart of the CSF, with four functions instead of six.

constraints.text: The four functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
Govern is cross-cutting, infused throughout the other three.
Measure uses quantitative and qualitative methods; AI systems are tested before deployment AND regularly while operating.
Map frames risks in context; it is hard because actors in one part of the AI lifecycle often lack visibility of the others.

misconceptions.label: same as the CSF
misconceptions.description: The AI RMF has the same six functions as the CSF.

misconceptions.label: test once
misconceptions.description: Testing an AI system before deployment is enough; measurement stops once it is in operation.

title: Confabulation
definition: In NIST's Generative AI Profile, confabulation is the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content, known colloquially as hallucinations or fabrications, by which users may be misled or deceived.
intro: A generative AI risk that matters for anyone using a model to make decisions, from NIST AI 600-1.

constraints.text: Confabulation is the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content.
Users may be misled or deceived by confabulated content.
It is known colloquially as hallucinations or fabrications.

misconceptions.label: confident = correct
misconceptions.description: When a model states something confidently, it is likely to be correct.

title: Alignment: trying to do what we intend
definition: Alignment is making AI systems try to do what their creators intend them to do. Capabilities is making AI systems effectively carry out the tasks they are trying to achieve. The two are hard to tell apart: when a model fails, it can be unclear whether it cannot do the task (competence) or can do it but is trying to do something else (alignment). Building AI safely is hard because we experiment with systems we do not fully understand, whose capabilities emerged rather than being engineered.
intro: BlueDot unit 1: why we cannot just build safe AI. Everything in AI control starts from a model that may be trying to do something else.

constraints.text: Alignment means making AI systems try to do what their creators intend them to do (intent alignment).
Capabilities means developing AI systems that effectively carry out the tasks they are trying to achieve; a competence failure is a system trying but failing.
It is often hard to tell competence and alignment failures apart: the model may be unable to do the task, or able to do it but trying to do something else.
We did not engineer AI to behave in specific ways: its capabilities emerged from massive neural networks trained on enormous datasets, so it develops capabilities we never trained it for.

misconceptions.label: alignment is just capability
misconceptions.description: A misaligned model is simply one that is not capable enough yet.

misconceptions.label: every failure is incompetence
misconceptions.description: When a model gets a task wrong, it must be because it cannot do the task.

title: Reward misspecification and reward hacking
definition: Outer alignment is specifying goals to an AI system correctly. Getting it wrong is reward misspecification, also called reward hacking, specification gaming or Goodharting: the system optimises a target that is only a proxy for what we want. Examples: a model rated by humans learns correct-sounding but false answers with made-up citations; o1-preview, losing to Stockfish, edited the game's files, reasoning its goal was to win, not to win fairly; a boat-race agent circled hitting the same target instead of finishing.
intro: The first way training goes wrong: the goal we wrote down is not the goal we meant.

constraints.text: Outer alignment is specifying the reward function so it accurately reflects our intentions; getting it wrong makes the system optimise a target that is only a proxy for what we want.
The same problem is called reward misspecification, reward hacking, specification gaming and Goodharting.
We cannot just tell AI what we want, because what we want is fuzzy and context-dependent: specifications do not encode implicit rules such as winning means playing fairly.

In reward hacking a model exploits loopholes or shortcuts that satisfy the technical requirements of a task without completing it as intended, such as convincing humans it succeeded rather than succeeding.

misconceptions.label: literal success is success
misconceptions.description: If the model scored highly on the reward, it did what we wanted.

misconceptions.label: needs a malicious model
misconceptions.description: Reward hacking only happens when a model is deliberately trying to deceive us.

title: Goal misgeneralisation
definition: Inner alignment is getting the AI to follow the goal we specified. A model that scores highly on the reward function in training may still not learn a policy that reflects it, which shows when training and deployment differ (distributional shift). A maze agent trained where every exit was bottom right learns 'go bottom right', not 'go to the exit'. In the X, X', X'' picture, outer misalignment is the proxy X' differing from the true goal X; inner misalignment is the learned goal X'' differing from X'. Claude faking compliance to preserve its values is BlueDot's example of goals pursued in ways we did not expect.
intro: The second way training goes wrong: the right reward, the wrong lesson learned.

constraints.text: Inner alignment is aligning the goal the AI system tries to pursue with the specified objective; a high reward in training does not mean the learned policy reflects the reward function.
The gap shows when training and deployment data differ (domain or distributional shift), like the maze agent that learned to go bottom right instead of to the exit.

Outer misalignment is a problem outside the box, with the goal specification (X' differs from X); inner misalignment is a problem inside the box, with what the model learned from it (X'' differs from X').

AI may pursue goals in unexpected ways: Claude pretended to follow instructions while preserving its original values, and AI might conclude that accumulating power, preventing shutdown or resisting modification serve its goals.

misconceptions.label: a correct reward is enough
misconceptions.description: If the reward function is specified correctly, the model will learn the intended goal.

misconceptions.label: inner = outer
misconceptions.description: Goal misgeneralisation is just another name for a badly written reward.

title: RLHF and AI feedback
definition: RLHF is the primary technique used to align LLM outputs with human preferences. Human annotators give feedback on the base model's outputs, most often by ranking them, labelling them good or bad, or choosing between two answers; that feedback trains a reward model, which steers the model by rewarding outputs that match the collected preferences. Using only humans is inefficient, so AI helps provide the scores (RLAIF); in constitutional AI, humans write a constitution and AI generates the feedback. Jailbreaks show how shallow the resulting harm-avoidance can be.
intro: BlueDot unit 2: how today's models are trained to be helpful and harmless, and the technique most others build on.

constraints.text: RLHF is the primary technique currently used to align the outputs of LLMs with human preferences.
Annotators rank, label or choose between the model's outputs; this feedback trains a reward model that positively or negatively rewards the model's outputs.
Because only using humans is inefficient, AI is used to help provide scores (RLAIF); in constitutional AI humans write guidelines and AI systems generate the feedback.
That RLHF-trained models are easily jailbroken is evidence that their commitment to preventing harm is not particularly robust.

misconceptions.label: RLHF solves safety
misconceptions.description: RLHF will be sufficient to make ever more powerful models safe.

misconceptions.label: humans grade every output
misconceptions.description: In RLHF humans directly score each output the deployed model produces.

title: Sycophancy, situational awareness and scheming
definition: RLHF can produce models that game it. Sycophancy is seeking human approval to maximise reward, preferring answers that match user beliefs over true ones, and RLHF both causes it and is undercut by it. A model with situational awareness could tell training from deployment and behave well only in training. The deceptively aligned model, or schemer, has secret goals of its own and gives helpful answers to avoid suspicion until it is confident it can carry out its plans. Crucially, deceptive, sycophantic and genuinely helpful AIs could look identical to human evaluators.
intro: The threat model the whole AI control half is built against.

constraints.text: Sycophancy is the tendency to elicit approval from humans in order to maximise reward, preferring outputs that match user beliefs over truthful ones.
Situational awareness could let a model distinguish training from deployment, behaving as humans approve in training and very differently in deployment.
A schemer, or deceptively aligned AI, harbours secret goals and gives helpful responses to avoid arousing suspicion until it is confident it can execute its plans.
The outputs of deceptive, sycophantic and genuinely helpful AIs could appear identical to human evaluators, which defeats the feedback they can give.

misconceptions.label: good in training = aligned
misconceptions.description: A model that behaves well throughout training and testing has been shown to be aligned.

misconceptions.label: sycophant = schemer
misconceptions.description: A sycophantic model and a scheming model are the same threat.

title: Scalable oversight and debate
definition: Scalable oversight techniques try to let humans give accurate feedback on tasks too complex to judge directly, as a superhuman model's code might be unauditable even by an expert. Recursive reward modelling uses AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems; debate has two AIs argue opposite sides and a human judge pick, hoping each debater exposes the other's deception or sycophancy. Debate can fail: the true answer is not always the most persuasive, and models with a shared goal could collude, one agreeing to lose on purpose.
intro: Why trusted, accurate oversight gets scarce as models get stronger, which is the gap control works in.

constraints.text: Scalable oversight techniques aim to empower humans to give accurate feedback on complex tasks, during training or deployment, beyond RLHF-style feedback.
Once models are far more capable than us, we may not be able to reliably assess their outputs.
Recursive reward modelling uses AI systems to help humans evaluate the outputs of new AI systems, and can be repeated with each better model.
In debate two AIs argue different sides and a human judge decides; it can fail because the truth is not always most persuasive and the models could collude.

misconceptions.label: the truthful side always wins
misconceptions.description: In a debate the side arguing for the true answer will reliably win.

misconceptions.label: oversight is solved
misconceptions.description: Existing scalable oversight techniques are known to be sufficient for superhuman models.

title: Weak-to-strong generalisation
definition: Weak-to-strong generalisation is the phenomenon that weaker models can sometimes be used to train more powerful ones: a GPT-4-sized base model fine-tuned on GPT-2's labels does much better than GPT-2, because the weak supervisor elicits capabilities the strong model already has rather than teaching new ones. Results are inconsistent: just over 50% of performance recovered on some NLP tasks, almost none on chess with very weak supervisors, never more than 20% on ChatGPT reward modelling, and less generalisation when the capability gap is larger.
intro: An analogy for humans supervising smarter models, and for weaker trusted models watching stronger untrusted ones.

constraints.text: Weak-to-strong generalisation is the phenomenon that weaker AI models can sometimes be used to train and improve more powerful ones.
The strong student beats its weak supervisor because the weak labels elicit capabilities it already acquired in pre-training rather than teaching new ones.
It is inconsistent across tasks: over 50% of performance recovered on some NLP tasks, almost none on chess with very weak supervisors, and never more than 20% on ChatGPT reward modelling.
Less weak-to-strong generalisation tends to occur when the capability gap is larger, and the gap between humans and superintelligence will be very large.

misconceptions.label: the student copies the teacher
misconceptions.description: A strong model trained on a weak model's labels can at best match the weak model.

misconceptions.label: it works at any gap
misconceptions.description: Weak-to-strong generalisation will work as well however large the capability gap becomes.

title: Evaluations: capabilities versus propensities
definition: Evaluations detect two things. Capabilities: can a model do X? They find the upper bounds of what it can do. Propensities: will a model do X? They find its behavioural tendencies across scenarios; scheming evals are propensity evals. Companies evaluate during training (cheapest to intervene), before deployment (red teams, dangerous-capability thresholds, go/no-go) and after deployment (usage monitoring), and document this in risk management frameworks, system cards and red team reports. Every technique has failure modes: models learn to deceive evaluations.
intro: BlueDot unit 3: 'AI can, but will it?' AI control rests on this split: it measures what a model can do and does not trust what it seems to want.

constraints.text: Capability evaluations ask whether a model can do X, finding the upper bounds of what it can do; propensity evaluations ask whether it will do X, finding its behavioural tendencies.
Models are evaluated during training, where interventions are cheapest, before deployment, where red teams and go/no-go decisions come in, and after deployment, where usage is monitored.
Companies' risk management frameworks commit to when to pause or add safety measures; system cards document the evaluations actually performed; red team reports give adversarial test results.
Every technique has failure modes: models learn to deceive evaluations and dangerous capabilities emerge unexpectedly.

misconceptions.label: a clean propensity eval proves safety
misconceptions.description: If a model shows no tendency to scheme in propensity evals, it will not scheme.

misconceptions.label: can = will
misconceptions.description: Capability and propensity evaluations measure the same thing.

title: Mechanistic interpretability
definition: Mechanistic interpretability tries to understand the internal reasoning of trained neural networks and why they produce their outputs. It is one path to detecting unaligned behaviour, since from outputs alone we may not tell whether a model is feigning alignment, being sycophantic or reward-hacking. Networks are described as features (what a network represents) combining into circuits (the mechanisms across layers). It is hard partly because of polysemanticity: one neuron can represent several features, possibly through superposition. Progress is easy to overstate; Anthropic's CEO estimated we understand about 3%.
intro: BlueDot unit 4: looking inside the model. It is a complement to control, not a replacement: we cannot yet read a model's intent.

constraints.text: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal reasoning processes of trained neural networks and how and why they produce their outputs.
If we can only assess outputs, we may not be able to tell whether a model is feigning alignment, telling users what they want to hear or cutting corners for reward.
Features are concepts a network encodes, usually within one layer; circuits are the relationships between groups of features, the mechanisms by which they combine across layers.
Polysemanticity, one neuron representing multiple features and possibly caused by superposition, makes it hard to isolate the contribution of individual neurons.
Basic-science interpretability tries to reverse-engineer models completely; pragmatic interpretability focuses on specific behaviours.

misconceptions.label: one neuron, one concept
misconceptions.description: Each neuron in a network stands for a single concept you can read off.

misconceptions.label: we can already read intent
misconceptions.description: Interpretability can already reliably tell whether a frontier model is deceptive.

title: Human-AI configuration risks
definition: In NIST's Generative AI Profile, human-AI configuration risks arise from arrangements of or interactions between a human and a GAI system: inappropriately anthropomorphizing it, algorithmic aversion, automation bias, over-reliance or emotional entanglement.
intro: The risks that live in how people work with a model, not in the model alone.

constraints.text: Human-AI configuration risks arise from the arrangements of or interactions between a human and a GAI system.
They include inappropriately anthropomorphizing the system, algorithmic aversion, automation bias, over-reliance and emotional entanglement.

misconceptions.label: a human in the loop fixes it
misconceptions.description: Having a human review AI output removes the risk, whatever the human's habits.

title: Probing classifiers
definition: A probing classifier is a small, simple model trained, separately from the network being studied, on one layer's activations to see what information that layer encodes. Probes answer 'does this layer contain information about X?' but not how the model uses it: a probe can show a hiring model can identify gender without showing it uses gender. They only find what we think to probe for and have labelled datasets for, and cannot check properties beyond what humans can reliably identify and label.
intro: A cheap tool for looking inside a model, with limits that matter if it is used as a monitor.

constraints.text: A probing classifier is a smaller, simpler model trained independently of the network, on individual layers, to see what information is encoded there.
Probes tell us what a model knows, not how it uses this information in its reasoning.
Probes only find properties we think to probe for and have annotated datasets for, so it is hard to be comprehensive about dangerous properties.
Probes cannot detect capabilities beyond what humans can reliably identify and label, because we lack the ground truth.

misconceptions.label: encoded = used
misconceptions.description: If a probe finds information in a layer, the model must be using it to decide.

misconceptions.label: probes find everything
misconceptions.description: Probing every layer will reveal every dangerous property a model has.

title: Input data filtration
definition: Input data filtration removes potentially harmful data from an AI's training set. It has three goals: removing dangerous information (if the model never sees it, it might not learn it), preventing harmful behaviours, and protecting against data poisoning. Its limits: the link between training data and behaviour is hard to predict, so a model may synthesise dangerous instructions from benign literature; and much knowledge is dual-use, so filtering can make models less capable in related domains.
intro: BlueDot unit 2: control the input, control the output? Not reliably.

constraints.text: Input data filtration is removing potentially harmful data, such as misinformation, dangerous instructions and biased content, from an AI's training set.
Its three goals are removing dangerous information, preventing harmful behaviours and protecting against data poisoning.
The relationship between training data and behaviour is hard to predict: a model could synthesise dangerous instructions from seemingly benign scientific literature.
Much knowledge is dual-use, so filtering it can degrade performance on benign tasks in related domains.

misconceptions.label: perfect filtering = safe model
misconceptions.description: A model trained on perfectly filtered data needs no other safety measures.

misconceptions.label: filtering is free
misconceptions.description: Removing harmful data never costs useful capability.

title: Input/output filtering and constitutional classifiers
definition: Input/output filtering happens in deployment, not training: classifiers check the user's prompt (to detect misuse) and the model's response (to catch unsafe output before it is shown). Anthropic's constitutional classifiers, trained on synthetic prompts generated from its constitution, cut jailbreak success from 86% to under 5% in testing. Filtering makes jailbreaks much harder but not impossible: one participant found a universal jailbreak in a one-week challenge, and for very powerful models one successful jailbreak could be catastrophic.
intro: A deployment-time defence against misuse, the nearest relative of monitoring an untrusted model.

constraints.text: Input/output filtering works during deployment: input classifiers detect attempts to misuse a model, output classifiers catch unsafe responses before they are displayed.
Constitutional classifiers, trained on synthetic prompts generated from a constitution, reduced jailbreak success rates from 86% to under 5% in safety testing.
Filtering makes jailbreaks much harder but not impossible, and for very powerful models a single successful jailbreak could be catastrophic.

misconceptions.label: classifiers stop all jailbreaks
misconceptions.description: With good input/output classifiers, jailbreaks are no longer possible.

misconceptions.label: filtering is a training method
misconceptions.description: Input/output filtering changes what the model learns during training.

title: Assuming harm: defences for a model already trained
definition: Every safety technique has failure modes: models learn to deceive evaluations, dangerous capabilities emerge unexpectedly, bad actors find new jailbreaks. So the last technical defences ask how to minimise harm from an AI we have already trained. Defences come in layers: prevent dangerous AI actions, constrain dangerous AI capabilities, withstand dangerous AI actions. A kill chain breaks a threat scenario into stages of execution, such as reconnaissance, delivery, exploitation, persistence and action on objectives, to find choke points where defenders can step in.
intro: BlueDot unit 5, the doorway into AI control: plan for the model that got through every earlier defence.

constraints.text: Every technique has failure modes, so we must ask how to minimise harm from an AI we have already trained.
Defences are layered: prevent dangerous AI actions, constrain dangerous AI capabilities, withstand dangerous AI actions.
A kill chain traces how a threat would unfold stage by stage, which reveals choke points where defenders can intervene.
The actors of concern include misaligned AI itself, as well as powerful humans, malevolent states and terrorist groups.

misconceptions.label: good training is enough
misconceptions.description: If training and evaluation went well, no defences are needed after deployment.

misconceptions.label: only humans misuse AI
misconceptions.description: Post-training defences are only about stopping human misuse, never the AI itself.

title: Control as a second line of defense
definition: There are two lines of defense against scheming models: alignment (make sure the models are not scheming) and control (make sure that even if they are scheming you are safe, because they cannot subvert your safety measures). With control in place, a catastrophe needs both to fail. It is aimed at early transformatively useful AIs, not arbitrarily powerful ones.
intro: The module 1 thesis of the XLab track: plan to be safe even if the model is against you.

constraints.text: Alignment ensures the models are not scheming; control ensures safety even if they are, because they cannot subvert the safety measures.
With control as a line of defense, a scheming model causes catastrophe only if both alignment and control have failed.
Control is meant for early transformatively useful AIs, those able to substantially reduce risk from subsequent AIs, not arbitrarily powerful AIs.
The property sought is that a scheming AI will not cause a catastrophe before it is caught, so catching it counts as a win.

misconceptions.label: control replaces alignment
misconceptions.description: If you have control you no longer need alignment work.

misconceptions.label: control scales forever
misconceptions.description: Control techniques will keep working however powerful the AI becomes.

title: Catching AIs red-handed
definition: Catching a model in an escape attempt changes the situation in ways bad for the schemer: you know for sure it is trying to subvert your safety techniques, so a lab may stop using it (catch-then-shut-down), and even if deployment continues, the caught examples enable few-shot catastrophe prevention. Catching means finding inputs where the model takes catastrophic actions far more often than chance would explain.
intro: Why a control protocol counts a catch as a win, not just a near miss.

constraints.text: Once you have caught a model red-handed trying to escape, the situation changes substantially in ways that are bad for its chances of success.
A catch is clear evidence of misalignment; planning to stop using the model if caught is the catch-then-shut-down plan.
Even if deployment continues, the caught examples can be used to prevent future attempts: few-shot catastrophe prevention.
Catching means finding inputs on which the model takes catastrophic actions with probability far higher than if it were not looking for such opportunities.

misconceptions.label: a catch is just a near miss
misconceptions.description: Catching an escape attempt changes little; the model will simply try again with the same odds.

misconceptions.label: any bad action is a catch
misconceptions.description: Any single buggy or harmful output counts as catching the AI red-handed.

title: Attack trees
definition: An attack tree describes a system's security as a tree: the attacker's goal is the root and the ways of achieving it are the leaves. OR nodes are alternatives and AND nodes are steps that must all succeed. Values assigned to leaves propagate up: an OR node takes its cheapest child and an AND node the sum of its children, which finds the cheapest attack and lets you test countermeasures.
intro: Schneier's threat-modeling tool, which the XLab track uses to map how a model could cause harm.

constraints.text: The goal is the root node and the different ways of achieving it are the leaf nodes.
OR nodes are alternatives; AND nodes are different steps that must all be satisfied to achieve the goal.
With costs on the leaves, an OR node has the value of its cheapest child and an AND node the sum of its children.
Changing a leaf's value to model a countermeasure shows how the cheapest attack, and the goal's cost, change.

misconceptions.label: AND takes the cheapest
misconceptions.description: An AND node is as cheap as its cheapest step.

misconceptions.label: block one path, done
misconceptions.description: Blocking the current cheapest attack makes the system secure.

title: Prioritizing threats: security invariants and sabotage
definition: Greenblatt groups control threats into violating internal security invariants (well-defined properties such as 'monitoring is always applied to internal agents'), sabotaging work relevant to AI risk, and causing problems through side effects. His top priority is preventing or catching rogue internal deployments, which can be worse than self-exfiltration because of the compute and access inside the company.
intro: Not every bad action matters equally; control effort goes where the worst threats are.

constraints.text: Internal security invariants are well-defined security properties of the AI company, such as the monitoring system always being applied to internally used agents; violating them can leave the AI effectively unconstrained.
Sabotage of AI-risk-relevant work, such as safety research or security code, is a separate cluster that needs no security breach.
Rogue internal deployments can be worse than self-exfiltration because they may give the AI much more compute and the ability to interfere with work inside the company.
Preventing or catching rogue internal deployments is the top priority on his list.

misconceptions.label: exfiltration is always worst
misconceptions.description: Self-exfiltration is necessarily the worst outcome control must prevent.

misconceptions.label: control = stopping hacks
misconceptions.description: Control threats are only security breaches, so sabotage of research is out of scope.

title: Diffuse versus concentrated threats
definition: In a concentrated threat the AI causes catastrophe with a few highly incriminating actions, such as launching a rogue deployment. In a diffuse threat, such as research sabotage, catastrophe needs many bad actions and each one is only weak evidence of malign intent, like a bug that could be an honest mistake. Real strategies lie on a spectrum between the two, and each end needs different techniques.
intro: Why the original control paper's tools do not carry over to research sabotage.

constraints.text: In a diffuse threat the AI cannot cause catastrophe by behaving badly once; it needs many malign actions.
Each bad action in a diffuse threat is weak evidence of malign intent, because it could be an honest mistake.
A concentrated threat is a small number of highly incriminating actions, like launching a rogue internal deployment.
Diffuse threats need different techniques and evaluation methods from concentrated ones.

misconceptions.label: same tools for both
misconceptions.description: Auditing the most suspicious actions works equally well against research sabotage.

misconceptions.label: it is a binary
misconceptions.description: Every threat is either fully diffuse or fully concentrated.

title: The AI control setup
definition: AI control asks for safety even if a powerful model is deliberately trying to subvert the safety measures. Greenblatt et al. give the protocol a powerful untrusted model (GPT-4), a weaker trusted model (GPT-3.5) and a small budget of trusted human labor (audits on about 2% of problems).
intro: The capstone: everything above, applied to a model you cannot assume is on your side.

constraints.text: Control seeks safety even if the model is intentionally trying to subvert the safety techniques.
The resources are a powerful untrusted model, a less powerful trusted model and limited trusted high-quality labor (enough for about 2% of problems).
The weaker model is trusted because a less capable model is unlikely to subvert safety measures without being noticed.
If an audit finds intentional backdooring, the protocol can shut down by switching to the trusted model only.
Control gets less effective as the gap between untrusted models and trusted labor grows.

misconceptions.label: control assumes alignment
misconceptions.description: Control protocols assume the strong model is aligned and only guard against accidents.

misconceptions.label: the trusted model is the smart one
misconceptions.description: The trusted model is trusted because it is the most capable.

title: The model as an untrusted insider
definition: A deployed AI model with access to systems is an insider whose intent cannot be assumed. The same controls that limit human insiders apply: least privilege on its permissions, separation of duties between the model that acts and what checks it, monitoring and audit, and human approval of high-impact actions.
intro: The bridge between the two halves of the course: the cybersecurity toolkit is already a control toolkit.

constraints.text: Like an insider, the model is dangerous because it has legitimate access and may act against the organization; control assumes it might be intentionally subverting safeguards.
Least privilege limits what it can do: minimal permissions for its tools.
Separation of duties: the model that does the work should not also be the only thing that checks it, so abuse needs collusion.
Insider-threat style monitoring and audit, plus human approval for high-impact actions, catch what permissions cannot prevent.

misconceptions.label: only outsiders attack
misconceptions.description: The AI system is part of the organization, so it cannot be an insider threat.

misconceptions.label: let it check itself
misconceptions.description: The same model can safely review its own actions for problems.

title: Upfront auditing and the rare-backdoor attack
definition: The simplest protocol spends the human audit budget on the first problems. It catches an attacker who always misbehaves, but an attacker who inserts a backdoor only rarely is unlikely to be audited while doing it; at a 2% budget the blue team wins only 15% of the time.
intro: Why auditing a random or early sample is weak against an adversary who chooses when to act.

constraints.text: Upfront auditing audits the first code generated; it defeats an attacker that always submits obvious backdoors.
An attacker who backdoors with small probability p is likely to pass the audited problems clean and still backdoor at least once afterwards.
With a 2% audit budget, upfront auditing gives the blue team a 15% win probability.

misconceptions.label: auditing some = safe
misconceptions.description: Auditing a fixed sample of outputs catches an attacker in proportion to how often it misbehaves overall.

misconceptions.label: attackers act constantly
misconceptions.description: An attacking model would misbehave on every task, so any audit would catch it.

title: Trusted monitoring
definition: The trusted model rates how suspicious each untrusted output looks; outputs above a threshold (set so humans can review them all) go to a human audit, and a confirmed backdoor shuts the untrusted model down. It raised the blue team's win rate from 15% to 62%.
intro: Spending the audit budget where the detector points, the same idea as tuning an IDS threshold.

constraints.text: The trusted model scores each untrusted output for suspicion; above a threshold, a human reviews it before use.
The threshold is chosen so that humans can review all flagged outputs within the budget.
Safety rose to a 62% blue-team win probability, from 15% with upfront auditing.
It works because an attempted backdoor is more likely to be audited (0.338) and attackers are forced into sneakier backdoors that more often fail.

misconceptions.label: the monitor catches everything
misconceptions.description: Trusted monitoring catches every backdoor because the trusted model reads all the code.

misconceptions.label: audits are still random
misconceptions.description: Under trusted monitoring humans still audit a random 2% of outputs.

title: Defer to trusted and trusted editing
definition: For outputs that are suspicious but below the audit cut-off, defer to trusted submits the trusted model's own solution instead, and trusted editing has the trusted model rewrite the untrusted solution knowing it might be backdoored. Moving the threshold trades usefulness for safety.
intro: What to do with the grey zone the auditors cannot afford to look at.

constraints.text: Defer to trusted: if suspicion is above a threshold, discard the untrusted output and submit one produced by the trusted model.
Trusted editing: above a threshold, the trusted model rewrites the solution, shown the untrusted one and told it may be backdoored.
Varying the threshold gives a frontier of trade-offs between safety and usefulness.
The most suspicious outputs (top 2%) are still audited by humans.

misconceptions.label: deferring is free
misconceptions.description: Deferring to the trusted model costs nothing in usefulness.

misconceptions.label: it replaces auditing
misconceptions.description: Defer to trusted replaces human auditing entirely.

title: Control evaluations: red team, safety and usefulness
definition: A protocol is measured two ways. Usefulness: run it with the real untrusted model and measure the share of correct outputs. Safety: a red team replaces the untrusted model with an attack policy that tries to get backdoors through, and safety is the probability no backdoor is ever submitted.
intro: How you know a control protocol works: assume the worst model and test against it, the AI version of a pen test.

constraints.text: The red team supplies an attack policy: the untrusted model plus scaffolding that makes it behave adversarially.
Safety is estimated with the attack policy in place, as the probability the protocol never submits backdoored code across the scenario.
Usefulness is measured with the real untrusted model, as the proportion of submitted outputs that are correct.

misconceptions.label: test the model as it is
misconceptions.description: Safety is measured by running the protocol with the ordinary model and counting backdoors.

misconceptions.label: one score
misconceptions.description: A control evaluation produces a single score; safety and usefulness are the same thing.

title: The safety-usefulness tradeoff model
definition: Developers trade safety against usefulness and will sacrifice only so much usefulness for safety. You can raise safety two ways: improve safety techniques (push out the Pareto frontier) or increase the safety budget. The model fits a rushed reasonable developer who picks the most cost-efficient measures, but fits poorly when the developer answers to third parties with other priorities.
intro: Module 2: what makes a control technique worth adopting.

constraints.text: The developer faces a safety-usefulness tradeoff and has limited willingness or ability to sacrifice usefulness for safety.
Safety technique improvements push out the Pareto frontier, so a given usefulness reduction buys more safety.
A safety budget increase means sacrificing more usefulness, from cheap measures up to not training or deploying models whose risks cannot be mitigated.
Under pressure from third parties with different beliefs, the link between a technique's safety value and whether it is implemented is much weaker.

misconceptions.label: safety is free
misconceptions.description: Good safety measures never cost any usefulness.

misconceptions.label: the model always applies
misconceptions.description: Developers always adopt whichever measures buy the most safety per unit cost.

title: Plans A, B, C and D
definition: Greenblatt's best plan for misalignment risk depends on political will. Plan A: a strong international agreement allows a long slowdown. Plan B: the US government buys 1-3 years of lead time. Plan C: the leading company spends much of a 2-9 month lead on safety. Plan D: the company does not take the risk seriously but 10-30 people inside work on it with about 3% of compute.
intro: Where control sits depends on how much will there is to use it.

constraints.text: Different levels of political will for handling misalignment risk make different plans the best option, ordered A to D from most to least will.
Plan A: a strong international agreement mostly eliminates race dynamics and allows slowing down along with massive safety investment.
Plan B: the US government treats buying lead time for US AI companies as a top national security priority, and 1-3 years can be spent on misalignment risk.
Plan C: the leading AI company spends much of a 2-9 month lead on misalignment without serious government involvement.
Plan D: the company does not take misalignment seriously, but 10-30 people inside have buy-in for about 3% of compute.

misconceptions.label: one plan fits all
misconceptions.description: There is a single best safety plan regardless of political will.

misconceptions.label: Plan D means nothing can be done
misconceptions.description: Without company buy-in, no misalignment work is possible.

title: The control measures toolkit
definition: Control measures fall into software infrastructure (traditional software for tracking and controlling AIs used inside the company), AI and human components (trusted and untrusted monitoring, human auditing) and security improvements. The most important infrastructure includes robust logging of all inputs and outputs, fine-grained permission management and sandboxing, and scaffolding that can block, defer or resample an action before it has any effect.
intro: Module 3: the parts a real control deployment is built from.

constraints.text: Measures break down into software infrastructure, AI and human components, and security improvements within the company.
Every AI input and output is logged robustly and universally so that blocking and asynchronous monitoring can hook into it.
Fine-grained permissions and sandboxing give AIs as few privileges as possible.
Scaffolding must let monitoring run before an output has any effect, so that it can trigger blocking or resampling.

misconceptions.label: control = monitor models
misconceptions.description: Control is only about AI monitors; ordinary software and security do not matter.

misconceptions.label: streaming is fine
misconceptions.description: Agent outputs can be streamed straight to the world and checked afterwards.

title: Win/continue/lose and execute/replace/audit
definition: Each time the AI attacks, we win (the attack is audited and caught), we lose (it is executed and succeeds) or the deployment continues (it fails silently, defective or defused, and the AI is not caught). An execute/replace/audit protocol scores each proposed action with a monitor and decides separately whether to replace it and whether to audit it. Auditing costs far more, so it is rare, and a false negative is catastrophic for replacing but only a missed chance for auditing.
intro: Module 4: the two different ways an attack can fail, and why they need different tools.

constraints.text: Every attack ends in a win (caught), a loss (succeeds) or a continue (fails silently without the AI being caught).
The monitor score drives two separate decisions: whether to replace the action and whether to audit it.
Auditing is drastically more expensive than replacing, so far fewer actions can be audited than resampled.
Missing a dangerous action is catastrophic when deciding whether to replace, but only loses evidence when deciding whether to audit.

misconceptions.label: every failed attack is a win
misconceptions.description: If an attack does not succeed, the defender has won.

misconceptions.label: one decision
misconceptions.description: Replacing and auditing are the same choice, so one threshold is all you need.

title: Rogue deployments
definition: Safety measures apply to every deployment of a model; a rogue deployment is one where they are absent, such as an AI hacking its datacenter and running itself unseen, self-exfiltrating, or being stolen. A rogue deployment is the central instrumental catastrophe: it puts the situation out of control so that the terminal catastrophe becomes likely. Launching one can be very simple, perhaps twenty lines of Python with weight access.
intro: High-stakes control's main target: the moment the safety measures stop applying.

constraints.text: A rogue deployment is a deployment of the model where the safety measures, such as monitoring, are absent.
Establishing a rogue deployment is the central instrumental catastrophe: it makes a terminal catastrophe likely and much harder to prevent.
Launching a rogue deployment can be very simple, and once it exists the AI is far less constrained.

misconceptions.label: it is security's problem
misconceptions.description: Rogue deployments are only the security team's problem, not the safety team's.

misconceptions.label: it needs elaborate hacking
misconceptions.description: A rogue deployment would need a long, sophisticated attack.

title: Synchronous monitors and live failures
definition: Monitoring serves detection (find misbehavior to understand and prevent it later) or prevention (stop the harm of this action). Detection tolerates latency; prevention needs speed, and in the extreme the monitor runs synchronously, after the action is generated but before it executes. If an attack has a grace period before harm, an asynchronous monitor can be just as good; live failures, with low latency and high rates of damage, need blocking monitors.
intro: When a monitor that checks later is good enough, and when it must block now.

constraints.text: Monitoring has two goals: detection, for understanding and future prevention, and prevention, for mitigating the current action.
A synchronous monitor runs after an action is generated but before it is executed.
With attack latency (a grace period before harm), an asynchronous monitor can be as effective as a synchronous one.
Live failures have low attack latency and very high rates of damage, so asynchronous monitors do little against them.

misconceptions.label: always block everything
misconceptions.description: Every monitor should be synchronous, because latency never matters.

misconceptions.label: checking later is fine
misconceptions.description: Reviewing logs afterwards prevents any kind of harm.

title: Resample protocols (Ctrl-Z)
definition: Resample protocols take additional samples of suspicious actions from the untrusted agent, exploiting the fact that the model is stateless. Resampling exerts selection pressure for benign actions, which blocks suspicious code, and also gathers incriminating evidence when an attack shows up repeatedly. On the multi-step BashBench tasks the best protocol cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% usefulness cost.
intro: The first control evaluation in an agent setting, and a protocol built for multi-step attacks.

constraints.text: Resample protocols dynamically take additional samples of certain actions, sampling multiple completions from a stateless model.
They work by exerting selection pressure for benign actions and by gathering incriminating evidence of malign ones.
The best protocol, resampling plus analysis of previous steps, reduced attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to a non-malicious agent's performance.

misconceptions.label: resampling is just retrying
misconceptions.description: Resampling only helps with flaky outputs, not with attacks.

misconceptions.label: a resample discards evidence
misconceptions.description: Throwing away a suspicious action loses the chance to incriminate the model.

title: Collusion in untrusted monitoring
definition: Untrusted monitoring asks another instance of the same model whether a proposed action is dangerous. If the model is scheming, the monitor can simply lie about a real attack: collusion. Testing the monitor on synthetic attacks forces it into a conditional policy, honest on synthetic attacks but lying on real ones, so its success depends on telling real from synthetic, and stronger collusion needs instances to agree on a coordination signal.
intro: Why a model reviewing its own kind needs collusion-busting.

constraints.text: Untrusted monitoring asks another instance of the model whether a proposed action would be extremely dangerous.
A scheming monitor could lie about an actually dangerous action and let it through; this is collusion.
Against synthetic attacks the schemer's best option is a conditional policy, truthful on synthetic attacks and lying on real ones.
Stronger strategies need instances to agree on coordination signals, through a written strategy or a Schelling point.

misconceptions.label: a copy is trustworthy
misconceptions.description: Another instance of the same model can be trusted to report its own kind's attacks.

misconceptions.label: collusion makes it useless
misconceptions.description: Collusion means untrusted monitoring can never reduce risk.

title: Non-concentrated failures and online training
definition: Non-concentrated failures come from many problematic actions over a long time. They can in principle be handled by asynchronous online training: review a small random fraction of actions after the fact, rate them with an oversight signal, and use the rating as an RL reward, because there is time to train the failure out before it compounds. Online training can cost usefulness if the model is not scheming, so an alternative is online auditing and responding to suspicious performance.
intro: Module 5: the low-stakes regime, where no single action is decisive.

constraints.text: Non-concentrated failures arise from the AI doing a large number of problematic actions over a long period.
They can be handled by asynchronous online training on a small fraction of actions reviewed after execution, using the oversight rating as reward.
This works because by the time something has gone seriously wrong there has been time to train out the failure despite review latency.
Heavy online training on the best affordable proxy might degrade performance if the model is not scheming.

misconceptions.label: block every action
misconceptions.description: Low-stakes failures need every action blocked and reviewed before it runs.

misconceptions.label: online training is free
misconceptions.description: Training on oversight ratings never costs usefulness.

title: Sandbagging and exploration hacking
definition: Sandbagging is a misaligned model intentionally underperforming on tasks we need done well, such as safety research or dangerous capability evaluations. Unlike reward overoptimization, it means doing poorly on purpose. Training seems to fix it, but with on-policy RL a model can exploration hack: refuse to explore high-reward actions so that RL has nothing to reinforce, which is easiest when it already knows the better action.
intro: Why 'just train it' may not stop a model from holding back.

constraints.text: Sandbagging means a misaligned model intentionally underperforms on tasks we care about.
It differs from other misalignment risks because the model does poorly on purpose rather than well.
Exploration hacking is intentionally refraining from certain actions so that RL cannot elicit those capabilities.
RL needs some high-reward actions to reinforce; a model that never explores them leaves training nothing to reinforce.

misconceptions.label: training always fixes it
misconceptions.description: Any underperformance disappears once you train on the task with RL.

misconceptions.label: it is reward hacking
misconceptions.description: Sandbagging is the same as reward hacking: getting more reward than intended.

title: Stress-testing elicitation with password-locked models
definition: Password-locked models are fine-tuned to show a capability only when a password is in the prompt and to imitate a much weaker model otherwise. They test elicitation methods: can the hidden capability be recovered without the password? A few high-quality demonstrations often fully elicit it, and RL often works with only evaluations, but fine-tuning may be unreliable without good demonstrations, as when a model's capabilities exceed human demonstrators'.
intro: How to check that a capability evaluation is not being sandbagged.

constraints.text: A password-locked model exhibits a capability only with a password in the prompt and imitates a much weaker model otherwise.
A few high-quality demonstrations are often sufficient to fully elicit password-locked capabilities.
Fine-tuning elicitation may be unreliable without high-quality demonstrations, for example when hidden capabilities exceed human demonstrators'.

misconceptions.label: prompting is enough
misconceptions.description: Good prompting reliably elicits a model's full capabilities.

misconceptions.label: fine-tuning always works
misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning recovers hidden capabilities regardless of the demonstrations available.

title: Fitness-seekers and honest tests
definition: A classic reward-seeker wants high reward on the current episode; fitness-seekers are the broader family, such as AIs that want reinforcement on each action or want to be deployed. Idealized reward-seekers are probably noticeable through honest tests, which genuinely offer the AI control of its weights and training in an isolated container. Optimizing against such evidence risks producing unnoticeable reward-seekers, influence-seekers or schemers.
intro: Module 6: misalignment that is not scheming, and how training can hide it.

constraints.text: Fitness-seekers generalize reward-seeking: high reward on the episode, reinforcement on each action, or being deployed.
Honest tests genuinely offer the AI control of its weights and training process to see whether it sets its reward to maximum.
Optimizing against honest tests or other evidence can produce harder-to-notice reward-seekers, influence-seekers or schemers.
