misconceptions.label: only schemers are dangerous
misconceptions.description: Reward-seeking AIs pose no takeover risk, so control is only about schemers.

misconceptions.label: train it away
misconceptions.description: Once a test catches reward-seeking, training against the test solves the problem.

title: Spillway motivations
definition: Flawed RL may select for misaligned motivations, some far more dangerous than others. Spillway design tries to make the most likely generalization of reward hacking a bespoke bundle of benign reward-seeking traits: a drive to score well on the current task that responds to the user's description of the scoring criteria. Unlike inoculation prompting, it shapes which reward-hacking motivations are salient going into RL.
intro: Steering which misalignment you get, like a dam releasing pressure through a safe channel.

constraints.text: Since flawed RL may select for misaligned motivations, developers should try to control which kind emerges.
The spillway is a drive to score well on the current task that is responsive to the user's description of the scoring criteria.
Spillway design differs from inoculation prompting by shaping which reward-hacking motivations are salient going into RL.

misconceptions.label: it makes the AI aligned
misconceptions.description: Spillway design produces an aligned AI with no reward-seeking.

misconceptions.label: it is inoculation prompting
misconceptions.description: Spillway design is another name for inoculation prompting.

title: Deals with early schemers
definition: Stastny, Järviniemi and Shlegeris consider deals with early misaligned AIs: too weak to have a good chance of taking over themselves, but able to help prevent takeover by more dangerous later AIs. Powerful AIs would need huge offers, but early ones may accept less. The central bottleneck is credible commitment; higher payoffs compensate, though implausible offers hurt credibility, and a foundation acting for the AIs could hold up our side.
intro: Paying a misaligned AI to help rather than sabotage.

constraints.text: The deals target early misaligned AIs that cannot take over themselves but could help prevent takeover by later AIs.
The central bottleneck is that humans may struggle to make credible commitments; higher payoffs can compensate, within plausibility.
A foundation with trustees representing the AIs means the AI has to trust the foundation rather than the lab.

misconceptions.label: deal with the strongest AI
misconceptions.description: Deals are most promising with the most powerful misaligned AIs.

misconceptions.label: promises are automatically credible
misconceptions.description: An AI will believe any offer the lab makes.

title: Prevalence
definition: Prevalence of a disease is the number of people affected by a condition divided by the total population.
intro: How much disease there is right now: every existing case, old and new, over everyone in the population.

constraints.text: Prevalence = number of people currently affected (existing cases) / total population.
It counts every existing case, old and new, not only newly diagnosed ones.
A one-time survey of a population measures prevalence (e.g. 150 hypertensive of 600 surveyed = 25%).

misconceptions.label: prevalence = new cases
misconceptions.description: Prevalence counts only the newly diagnosed cases.

misconceptions.label: divide by people at risk
misconceptions.description: Prevalence divides by the population at risk, excluding people already affected.

title: Incidence
definition: Incidence is the number of new cases divided by the population at risk, so it does not include people already affected.
intro: How fast new disease appears: new cases over a period, among people who could still get it.

constraints.text: Incidence = number of new cases (in a period, e.g. a year) / population at risk.
The denominator is the population at risk, so people already affected are left out (e.g. 300/996,000 when 4,000 of 1,000,000 already have the disease).
A one-time screening finds existing cases, so it gives prevalence but cannot give incidence.

misconceptions.label: divide by the whole population
misconceptions.description: Incidence divides new cases by the total population, including people who already have the disease.

misconceptions.label: incidence = all cases
misconceptions.description: Incidence counts everyone who currently has the disease.

title: Chronic diseases: prevalence above incidence
definition: Chronic conditions generally have prevalences much higher than incidences because each case is counted in the incidence statistic only once but remains counted in the prevalence statistic for years.
intro: Long diseases pile up in prevalence.

constraints.text: Chronic conditions have prevalence much higher than incidence because each case is counted once in incidence but stays in prevalence for years.

misconceptions.label: chronic = equal
misconceptions.description: A lifelong condition like HIV has a prevalence about equal to its incidence.

title: Short diseases: prevalence close to incidence
definition: For prevalence and incidence to be close to each other the disease duration must be short: almost all patients with an acute condition recover quickly, so they are counted only once for both prevalence and incidence.
intro: Quick-to-clear diseases come and go within the year.

constraints.text: Short (acute) diseases such as strep throat or UTI have prevalence close to incidence, because patients recover within the same period.

misconceptions.label: acute = high prevalence
misconceptions.description: An acute infection like strep throat has a prevalence much higher than its incidence.

title: Better survival raises prevalence
definition: Increased survival would lead to the increased prevalence of the disease: as people affected by the disease live longer and new cases are being diagnosed, the total number of people with the condition increases.
intro: The most-tested twist on Step 3: a new treatment arrives. What happens to prevalence?

constraints.text: Better treatment that improves survival keeps cases counted for longer, so prevalence rises.
Incidence counts newly diagnosed cases, so improved management does not change it.

misconceptions.label: treatment lowers incidence
misconceptions.description: A better treatment lowers incidence because fewer people have the disease.

misconceptions.label: better survival lowers prevalence
misconceptions.description: If patients survive longer, prevalence falls.

title: Removing a risk factor
definition: If a risk factor (such as smoking) is eliminated it is going to lead to a decreased incidence of the disease.
intro: A smoking ban: fewer people become cases.

constraints.text: Removing a risk factor means fewer new cases, so incidence falls.
Without any change in treatment, prevalence then falls too.

misconceptions.label: risk factor = prevalence only
misconceptions.description: Eliminating a risk factor lowers prevalence but leaves incidence unchanged.

title: A lower diagnostic cut-off raises incidence and prevalence
definition: Changing the definition so that more people would be seen as positive would increase both prevalence and incidence of the disease in question.
intro: Move the line, and more people become cases.

constraints.text: Widening the disease definition (lower cut-off) raises both incidence and prevalence.

misconceptions.label: definition = incidence only
misconceptions.description: Lowering the cut-off raises incidence but leaves prevalence unchanged.

title: Case fatality rate
definition: Case fatality rate is the percentage of patients who die from the disease among those who have been affected.
intro: Of the people who have the disease, how many die of it?

constraints.text: Case fatality rate = deaths from the disease / people affected by it.

misconceptions.label: CFR over the population
misconceptions.description: Case fatality rate divides deaths by the total population.

title: Disease-specific mortality
definition: The disease-specific mortality is the number of deaths that can be attributed to the disease divided by the total population.
intro: Deaths from the disease over everyone, sick or not.

constraints.text: Disease-specific mortality = deaths attributed to the disease / total population.
Mortality can be built from incidence and CFR: e.g. 15% of an incidence of 600/100,000 = 90/100,000.

misconceptions.label: mortality over cases
misconceptions.description: Disease-specific mortality divides deaths by the number of people with the disease.

title: The diagnostic 2x2 table
definition: Comparing a new test with the gold standard sorts every person into true positive, false positive, false negative or true negative.
intro: Every diagnostic-test number on Step 3 comes from these four cells; read them off before any formula.

constraints.text: A false positive tested positive on the new test but was later determined not to have the disease (gold standard negative).
A false negative tested negative but was later found to have the disease.
True positives test positive and are affected; true negatives test negative and are confirmed unaffected.
Affected = TP + FN; unaffected = TN + FP.

misconceptions.label: false positive = missed case
misconceptions.description: A false positive is a person with the disease whom the test missed.

misconceptions.label: the new test is the truth
misconceptions.description: Cells are defined by the new test alone, not by the gold standard.

title: Sensitivity
definition: Sensitivity is the probability that the test is positive when the disease is present: the proportion of people affected who test positive, TP/(TP+FN).
intro: Read down the disease-present column: of the sick, how many does the test catch?

constraints.text: Sensitivity = proportion of people affected who test positive = TP/(TP+FN).
High sensitivity means few false negatives.
It is conditioned on having the disease, not on the test result.

misconceptions.label: sensitivity = P(disease | positive)
misconceptions.description: Sensitivity is the chance that a person who tests positive has the disease.

misconceptions.label: TP/(TP+FP)
misconceptions.description: Sensitivity is TP/(TP+FP).

title: Specificity
definition: Specificity is the probability that the test is negative when the disease is absent: the proportion of unaffected people who test negative, TN/(TN+FP).
intro: Read down the disease-absent column: of the healthy, how many does the test clear?

constraints.text: Specificity = proportion of unaffected people who test negative = TN/(TN+FP).
Highly specific tests have low false-positive rates, so a positive result can be trusted.
It is conditioned on not having the disease.

misconceptions.label: specificity = P(healthy | negative)
misconceptions.description: Specificity is the chance that a person who tests negative is healthy.

misconceptions.label: TN/(TN+FN)
misconceptions.description: Specificity is TN/(TN+FN).

title: Positive predictive value
definition: The positive predictive value represents the likelihood that the person who tests positive for a disease is actually affected: TP/(TP+FP).
intro: The patient's question after a positive result: do I really have it?

constraints.text: PPV = TP/(TP+FP): probability that a person who tests positive has the condition.
A PPV of 87% means a 13% chance that a positive patient does not have the disease.

misconceptions.label: PPV = sensitivity
misconceptions.description: PPV is the probability that a sick person tests positive.

misconceptions.label: PPV = accuracy
misconceptions.description: A PPV of 87% means the test is 87% accurate.

title: Negative predictive value
definition: The negative predictive value represents the likelihood that the person who tests negative is unaffected: TN/(TN+FN).
intro: The patient's question after a negative result: am I really clear?

constraints.text: NPV = TN/(TN+FN): probability that a person who tests negative does not have the disease.

misconceptions.label: NPV = specificity
misconceptions.description: NPV is the probability that a healthy person tests negative.

title: Predictive values depend on prevalence
definition: Sensitivity and specificity are inherent features of a test; PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence. Higher prevalence raises PPV and lowers NPV.
intro: Why the same test means different things in a 75-year-old smoker and a healthy 25-year-old.

constraints.text: Sensitivity and specificity are inherent properties of the test and do not change with prevalence.
Increasing prevalence increases PPV: people are more likely to have the disease regardless of how they test.
Increasing prevalence decreases NPV; at low prevalence NPV is high.

misconceptions.label: prevalence changes sensitivity
misconceptions.description: A more common disease makes the test more sensitive.

misconceptions.label: prevalence raises PPV and NPV
misconceptions.description: Higher prevalence raises both predictive values.

title: Screening tests: high sensitivity
definition: The higher the sensitivity of the test, the better it is as a screening test: the goal of screening is to identify all patients with the condition, even at the expense of some false positive results.
intro: A screen must miss almost no one.

constraints.text: A screening test should be highly sensitive: it must identify almost all affected people (lowest possible false negative rate), even at the cost of false positives.

misconceptions.label: screen with specificity
misconceptions.description: Screening tests should be the most specific available.

misconceptions.label: screen by PPV
misconceptions.description: The best screening test is the one with the highest PPV.

title: Confirmatory tests: high specificity
definition: The higher the specificity of the test, the better the test is for confirming the diagnosis: confirmatory tests are best when the rate of false-positives is as low as possible.
intro: A confirmation must almost never call a healthy person sick.

constraints.text: A confirmatory test should be highly specific: few false positives, so a positive patient very likely has the disease.

misconceptions.label: confirm with sensitivity
misconceptions.description: The best confirmatory test is the most sensitive one.

title: Ordering tests: screen, then confirm
definition: The appropriate order of tests is from more sensitive to more specific tests: sensitive tests are good for screening, while specific tests are used for confirmation.
intro: Two tests, one strategy: which goes first?

constraints.text: Run the more sensitive test first, then the more specific one to confirm.

misconceptions.label: specific test first
misconceptions.description: Start with the most specific test, then use the sensitive one to confirm.

title: Moving the cut-off
definition: Changing a test's cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity: calling more results positive raises sensitivity and lowers specificity; a stricter cut-off does the opposite.
intro: A lab threshold or lesion size moves: who becomes positive, and what happens to false negatives and false positives?

constraints.text: Widening the definition of positive (more people test positive) increases sensitivity and decreases specificity: fewer false negatives, more false positives.
A stricter cut-off (e.g. only lesions > 3 cm) gives more false negatives and fewer false positives: sensitivity falls, specificity rises.
How a test result is interpreted does not change the incidence of the disease.

misconceptions.label: a better cut-off raises both
misconceptions.description: Moving the cut-off can raise sensitivity and specificity together.

misconceptions.label: cut-off changes incidence
misconceptions.description: Raising the test's cut-off lowers the disease's incidence.

title: Relative risk
definition: Relative risk is the risk of developing a disease among people exposed to a risk factor divided by the risk in the unexposed. RR = 1 means equal risk; RR > 1 a risk factor; RR < 1 protective.
intro: The cohort study's answer: how many times more likely the exposed are to get the disease.

constraints.text: RR = risk of disease in the exposed / risk in the unexposed.
RR of 1 = no association; RR > 1 = risk factor; RR < 1 = protective.
Relative risk is calculated in cohort studies (incidence in exposed vs unexposed).

misconceptions.label: RR = difference in risk
misconceptions.description: Relative risk is the exposed risk minus the unexposed risk.

misconceptions.label: RR from case-control
misconceptions.description: A case-control study gives relative risk directly.

title: Odds ratio
definition: The odds ratio compares the odds of exposure among cases with the odds of exposure among controls: (exposed cases/unexposed cases) / (exposed controls/unexposed controls) = ad/bc.
intro: The case-control study's answer, from a 2x2 table of exposure by disease.

constraints.text: OR = odds of exposure among cases / odds of exposure among controls.
Odds of exposure among cases = exposed affected / unexposed affected; among controls = exposed unaffected / unexposed unaffected; OR = (a*d)/(b*c), e.g. (40*85)/(60*15).
(exposed affected/all exposed) over (unexposed affected/all unexposed) is relative risk, not the odds ratio.

misconceptions.label: OR uses risks
misconceptions.description: The odds ratio divides the proportion of exposed who got sick by the proportion of unexposed who got sick.

misconceptions.label: OR = (a*b)/(c*d)
misconceptions.description: The odds ratio multiplies the cells across each row.

title: Attributable risk
definition: Attributable risk is the difference in risk between the exposed and unexposed groups, e.g. 15% - 5% = 10%.
intro: The absolute extra risk that comes with the exposure.

constraints.text: Attributable risk = risk in the exposed minus risk in the unexposed (a difference, not a ratio).
With 15% risk in smokers and 5% in non-smokers, AR = 10%.

misconceptions.label: AR is a ratio
misconceptions.description: Attributable risk is the risk in the exposed divided by the risk in the unexposed.

misconceptions.label: AR = 300%
misconceptions.description: From 15% versus 5%, the attributable risk is 300%.

title: Absolute risk reduction
definition: Absolute risk reduction represents the difference in risk (10% - 5% = 5%).
intro: How many percentage points of risk the treatment takes away.

constraints.text: ARR = risk in control - risk in treated (a difference).

misconceptions.label: ARR = proportion
misconceptions.description: Absolute risk reduction is the fraction of the risk that disappeared (10% to 5% = 50%).

title: Relative risk reduction
definition: Relative risk reduction refers to what proportion of the risk has disappeared following the intervention (10% to 5% = 50%).
intro: Same trial, a bigger-sounding number: the drug company quotes the RRR, the patient lives the ARR.

constraints.text: RRR = ARR / risk in control (a proportion): 12% to 8% is a 4% ARR and a 33% RRR.

misconceptions.label: ARR = RRR
misconceptions.description: Absolute and relative risk reduction are two names for the same number.

misconceptions.label: RRR = difference
misconceptions.description: Relative risk reduction is 12% - 8% = 4%.

title: Number needed to treat
definition: Number needed to treat refers to the number of patients who need to receive an intervention in order for 1 patient to be helped.
intro: Turning a risk difference into patients: how many to treat for one to benefit.

constraints.text: NNT = number of patients who need to receive the intervention for 1 patient to be helped.
NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction, rounded up: an ARR of 4% (12% to 8%) gives NNT = 1/0.04 = 25.

misconceptions.label: NNT = 1/RRR
misconceptions.description: NNT is one over the relative risk reduction.

misconceptions.label: NNT from RR
misconceptions.description: NNT is one over the relative risk.

title: Number needed to harm
definition: Number needed to harm represents the number of patients who need to be exposed to a risk factor for 1 patient to be harmed.
intro: The same count for a harm: how many exposed for one to be hurt.

constraints.text: NNH = number of patients who need to be exposed to a risk factor for 1 patient to be harmed.
NNH = 1 / attributable risk (the risk difference), rounded up.

misconceptions.label: NNH from RR
misconceptions.description: NNH is one over the relative risk.

title: Cohort studies
definition: Cohort studies divide participants by exposure to a risk factor and follow them for development of an effect, to determine relative risk. Prospective ones start now; retrospective ones start in the past and finish much faster.
intro: Exposure first, outcome later. The design behind relative risk.

constraints.text: Participants are grouped by exposure (exposed vs unexposed) and followed over time for the outcome.
A cohort study determines the relative risk (incidence in exposed vs unexposed).
A retrospective cohort starts in the past; its advantage is a much shorter timeframe than a prospective cohort.

misconceptions.label: grouped by disease
misconceptions.description: A cohort study starts by choosing people with and without the disease.

misconceptions.label: retrospective = case-control
misconceptions.description: Any study that looks back in time is a case-control study.

title: Case-control studies
definition: Case-control studies start from people with the disease (cases) and similar people without it (controls) and compare their odds of past exposure: they give the odds ratio.
intro: Outcome first, look back for exposure. The design for rare diseases, and the home of recall bias.

constraints.text: Participants are selected by disease status (cases vs controls with similar baseline characteristics), then past exposure is compared.
A case-control study gives the odds ratio: odds of exposure among cases / odds of exposure among controls.
It does not follow participants over time.

misconceptions.label: case-control gives RR
misconceptions.description: A case-control study reports relative risk.

misconceptions.label: grouped by exposure
misconceptions.description: A case-control study starts by choosing exposed and unexposed people.

title: Cross-sectional studies
definition: Cross-sectional studies determine the prevalence of a disease (and of a risk factor) in a population at one time; they do not establish causality.
intro: A snapshot: who has the disease and the exposure right now.

constraints.text: A cross-sectional study determines prevalence: the frequency of the disease and the risk factor at one point in time.
It cannot establish causality (no temporal sequence between exposure and outcome).

misconceptions.label: cross-sectional gives incidence
misconceptions.description: A cross-sectional study measures the rate of new cases.

misconceptions.label: snapshot proves cause
misconceptions.description: A strong association in a cross-sectional study shows the exposure causes the disease.

title: Randomized controlled trials
definition: A randomized controlled clinical trial randomly assigns patients to one of two interventions (or treatment vs placebo) and compares the outcomes; clinical trials require an active intervention.
intro: The only design where the investigator assigns the exposure.

constraints.text: Patients are randomly assigned to interventions (or treatment vs placebo / current standard of care) and outcomes are compared.
A clinical trial requires an active intervention; when giving the exposure would be unethical, an observational design is used instead.
Blinding participants and researchers protects the trial against observer bias and placebo effects.

misconceptions.label: observing a prescribed drug is a trial
misconceptions.description: Following patients already taking a drug for another reason is a clinical trial.

misconceptions.label: randomize any exposure
misconceptions.description: An RCT can assign a harmful exposure like second-hand smoke.

title: Meta-analysis
definition: A meta-analysis pools summary data from multiple studies and analyzes them together for more precise results and higher power; its quality depends on the quality of the studies pooled.
intro: Useful for rare conditions; garbage in, garbage out.

constraints.text: Meta-analysis pools data (and subjects) from multiple studies, giving more precise results and much higher power; it is mainly useful for rare conditions.
Its quality depends on the quality of the individual studies: biased studies give a biased meta-analysis.

misconceptions.label: pooling removes bias
misconceptions.description: Pooling many studies cancels out the biases of the individual studies.

misconceptions.label: meta-analysis is low powered
misconceptions.description: Meta-analyses have less power than a single large study.

title: Phase I trials
definition: In phase I of the clinical trial a small number of healthy volunteers is given a drug to assess its safety, toxicity profile, pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics.
intro: The first people to get a new drug: is it safe, and what does the body do with it?

constraints.text: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers; safety, toxicity, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

misconceptions.label: dosing in phase I
misconceptions.description: Optimal dosing is set in phase I with healthy volunteers.

title: Phase II trials
definition: In phase II a moderate number of patients is treated with the drug to assess its efficacy, optimal dosing and common side effects.
intro: Now patients with the disease: does it work, and at what dose?

constraints.text: Phase II: moderate number of patients with the disease; efficacy, optimal dosing and common side effects.
Comparing the drug to placebo or the current standard of care only occurs after phase II, in phase III.

misconceptions.label: comparison in phase II
misconceptions.description: Comparison with the current standard of care happens in phase II.

title: Phase III trials
definition: In phase III a large number of patients is randomly assigned to treatment and placebo (or previously used gold standard treatment) groups, comparing their outcomes with those of patients treated with the new drug.
intro: The big randomized head-to-head before approval.

constraints.text: Phase III: large number of patients randomized to the new drug vs placebo or current standard of care.

misconceptions.label: phase III in volunteers
misconceptions.description: Phase III gives the drug to healthy volunteers.

title: Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance
definition: Phase IV refers to surveillance after the treatment is approved in order to detect rare or long-term adverse effects which can lead to the drug being withdrawn from the market.
intro: After approval: the rare and late harms only thousands of patients reveal.

constraints.text: Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance for rare or long-term adverse effects, which can lead to withdrawal from the market.

misconceptions.label: lower the dose
misconceptions.description: A serious rare side effect found after release is handled by lowering the dose.

title: Selection bias
definition: Selection bias refers to nonrandom sampling of study participants.
intro: Who gets into the study is not representative.

constraints.text: Selection bias refers to nonrandom sampling (selection) of study participants.
Blinding has no effect on it.

misconceptions.label: blinding fixes selection
misconceptions.description: Blinding the investigators removes selection bias.

title: Attrition bias
definition: Attrition bias is a form of selection bias. It occurs when a large number of participants are lost to follow up and the majority of them are from the same group, altering the findings in the study.
intro: Who stays in the study is not representative.

constraints.text: Attrition bias: many participants lost to follow-up, mostly from one group, alters the findings.

misconceptions.label: loss to follow-up = recall bias
misconceptions.description: Losing participants to follow-up is a kind of recall bias.

title: Berkson bias
definition: Berkson bias refers to the tendency of hospitalized patients to be less healthy and have different exposures when compared to the general population.
intro: Hospital patients are not the general population.

constraints.text: Berkson bias: hospitalized patients are less healthy and have different exposures than the general population.

misconceptions.label: Berkson = recall
misconceptions.description: Berkson bias is hospitalized patients misremembering their exposures.

title: Recall bias
definition: Recall bias: people who develop a disease tend to remember and overreport their exposure compared with controls. It is a feature of case-control and other retrospective studies that depend on patients' recall.
intro: Cases search their memory harder than controls do.

constraints.text: Affected people are more likely to remember and overreport exposure to a risk factor than controls.
It is common in case-control and retrospective studies (surveys, questionnaires) that depend on recall.

misconceptions.label: recall bias in prospective cohorts
misconceptions.description: Recall bias is the main threat in a prospective cohort that measures exposure at baseline.

misconceptions.label: recall = observer bias
misconceptions.description: Recall bias is the researcher's memory distorting the data.

title: Observer bias
definition: Observer bias occurs when the researcher's strong belief in the existence or non-existence of an association affects the way the data is analyzed.
intro: The researcher's belief changes the reading.

constraints.text: Observer bias: the researcher's strong belief in (or knowledge of) the association or the treatment groups affects how the data are interpreted.

misconceptions.label: observer = participants watched
misconceptions.description: Observer bias is patients changing behaviour because they are watched.

title: Blinding
definition: Blinding refers to the unawareness of study participants (and/or researchers) as to whether they are receiving the treatment or not; blinding in clinical trials prevents observer bias.
intro: Nobody knows who got the drug, so nobody's expectations change the result.

constraints.text: Blinding (participants and/or researchers unaware of who receives treatment) prevents observer bias.
Unblinded patients who know they get a drug may report improvement through the placebo effect.

misconceptions.label: blinding fixes selection
misconceptions.description: Blinding stops nonrandom selection of participants.

title: Measurement bias
definition: Measurement bias occurs when faulty equipment leads to incorrect readings and therefore biased study results.
intro: A bad instrument: the reading itself is wrong.

constraints.text: Measurement bias occurs when faulty equipment (or inappropriate data collection) leads to incorrect readings.

misconceptions.label: measurement = researcher belief
misconceptions.description: Measurement bias is the researcher's belief changing the analysis.

title: Procedure bias
definition: Procedure bias occurs when participants are not treated equally.
intro: Unequal handling: one group gets treated differently from the other.

constraints.text: Procedure bias occurs when participants are not treated equally.

misconceptions.label: procedure = selection
misconceptions.description: Procedure bias is choosing participants nonrandomly.

title: Confounding
definition: A confounder is an external variable related to both the risk factor and the disease that distorts the real association between them (e.g. smoking behind a TV-watching and bladder cancer link).
intro: The third variable that makes an innocent exposure look guilty.

constraints.text: A confounder is related to both the exposure (cause) and the outcome (effect).
It changes the apparent association, so a non-causal exposure can look associated with the disease.
If people who watch more TV also smoke more, TV can falsely appear to cause bladder cancer.

misconceptions.label: related to one side only
misconceptions.description: A variable related only to the outcome is a confounder.

misconceptions.label: confounding = faulty equipment
misconceptions.description: Confounding is an error in how a variable was measured.

title: Lead-time bias
definition: Lead-time bias refers to the appearance of increased survival with early diagnosis that is not due to improved patient outcomes but rather purely due to an earlier date of disease detection.
intro: Diagnosing earlier starts the survival clock earlier.

constraints.text: Lead-time bias: apparent survival increase due only to an earlier date of detection, without improved outcomes.
If a disease is diagnosed at birth anyway (e.g. cystic fibrosis), lead-time bias cannot explain longer survival.

misconceptions.label: earlier detection = longer life
misconceptions.description: Detecting a disease earlier always means patients truly live longer.

title: Length-time bias
definition: Length-time bias refers to the tendency of screening studies to better identify diseases with longer latency periods.
intro: Screening catches the slow cases, which do better anyway.

constraints.text: Length-time bias: screening better identifies diseases with longer latency (slower progression).

misconceptions.label: length = lead
misconceptions.description: Length-time bias is survival looking longer because diagnosis came earlier.

title: Hawthorne effect
definition: The Hawthorne effect is a behavioral change in participants who know they are being followed (e.g. smokers who are followed stopping or cutting down).
intro: Being watched changes what people do.

constraints.text: Participants who know they are being studied change their behaviour.
Followed smokers may stop or decrease smoking, a known risk factor for coronary disease, so the study can miss the association.

misconceptions.label: Hawthorne = observer bias
misconceptions.description: The Hawthorne effect is the researcher's beliefs changing the interpretation.

misconceptions.label: Hawthorne = recall
misconceptions.description: The Hawthorne effect is participants misremembering exposures.

title: The mean
definition: The mean value is the sum of all the measured values divided by the number of measurements.
intro: Add them up, divide by how many.

constraints.text: Mean = sum of all values / number of values.

misconceptions.label: median = average
misconceptions.description: The mean is the middle value of the sorted list.

title: The median
definition: The median measurement is the one that has an equal number of measurements greater and lesser than it; with an even number of measurements, it is the average of the two middle values.
intro: Sort them; take the middle one.

constraints.text: Median = the middle value, with equal numbers above and below; with an even count, the average of the two middle values.

misconceptions.label: median = average
misconceptions.description: The median is the average of all the values.

title: The mode
definition: The mode is the most frequently encountered value.
intro: The value you see most often.

constraints.text: Mode = the most frequently occurring value.

misconceptions.label: mode = middle
misconceptions.description: The mode is the value in the middle of the sorted list.

title: Outliers
definition: A value that differs significantly from the usual measurements affects the mean the most, the median significantly less and the mode the least.
intro: One extreme value: which summary moves, and by how much?

constraints.text: An outlier affects the mean the most, the median less, and the mode the least (usually not at all).

misconceptions.label: median is most affected
misconceptions.description: An extreme value moves the median more than the mean.

title: Positively skewed distributions
definition: Positively skewed distributions are the ones where mean is larger than the median, which is larger than the mode.
intro: A tail of high values drags the mean up past the median.

constraints.text: Positively (right) skewed: mean > median > mode.

misconceptions.label: positive skew = mean < median
misconceptions.description: In a positively skewed distribution the mean is smaller than the median.

title: Negatively skewed distributions
definition: Negatively skewed distributions are the opposite of positively skewed ones: the mean is smaller than the median, which is smaller than the mode.
intro: A tail of low values drags the mean down below the median.

constraints.text: Negatively (left) skewed: mean < median < mode.

misconceptions.label: negative skew = mean > median
misconceptions.description: In a negatively skewed distribution the mean is larger than the median.

title: Bimodal distributions
definition: A bimodal distribution has two peaks: ulcerative colitis tends to occur either in young adults or in the elderly, with relatively few cases in middle age.
intro: Two separate humps on the curve.

constraints.text: Bimodal: two peaks (e.g. ulcerative colitis in young adults and the elderly).

misconceptions.label: two peaks = skew
misconceptions.description: A disease common in the young and the old gives a skewed distribution.

title: The normal distribution and SDs
definition: In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD, so about 16% lie beyond 1 SD and 2.5% beyond 2 SD on each side.
intro: Turn a value into SDs from the mean, then into a percentage of people.

constraints.text: About 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.
So about 16% lie beyond 1 SD on each side, and about 2.5% beyond 2 SD on each side.
Convert to SDs first: with mean 90 and SD 10, >110 is beyond 2 SD, about 2.5% (25 of 1000).

misconceptions.label: 5% beyond 2 SD on one side
misconceptions.description: About 5% of values lie more than 2 SD above the mean.

misconceptions.label: 32% beyond 1 SD on one side
misconceptions.description: About 32% of values lie more than 1 SD below the mean.

title: Combining probabilities
definition: The probability of an event that happens to a fraction of a fraction is the product: 5% of the 20% who bleed is 1% overall.
intro: Chain the percentages, or imagine 1,000 patients.

constraints.text: A fraction of a subgroup is the product of the two fractions: 5% of 20% = 1%.
Checking with a cohort of 1,000: 200 bleed, 5% of those = 10, so 10/1000 = 1/100.

misconceptions.label: take the smaller
misconceptions.description: The overall risk is just the 5%.

title: The null hypothesis
definition: The null hypothesis is the hypothesis of no relationship: it states that no difference exists.
intro: Every test starts by assuming nothing is going on.

constraints.text: The null hypothesis states there is no association or difference (e.g. no association between paracetamol use and pancreatitis).
The null is defined before the study; the study then tests it and it is either accepted or rejected.

misconceptions.label: null = the expected effect
misconceptions.description: The null hypothesis is that the drug works.

misconceptions.label: set the null afterwards
misconceptions.description: The null hypothesis is chosen after looking at the results.

title: The alternative hypothesis
definition: The alternative hypothesis is the hypothesis of some relationship: it states that a difference does exist.
intro: What the study hopes to show: something is going on.

constraints.text: The alternative hypothesis states that an association or difference exists.

misconceptions.label: alternative = no difference
misconceptions.description: The alternative hypothesis states that the drug and placebo do not differ.

title: Type I error
definition: Type I errors refer to rejecting a correct null hypothesis (eg, concluding that there is a difference between the two groups when in fact there is none).
intro: Seeing a difference that is not there.

constraints.text: Type I error: rejecting a correct null hypothesis, concluding there is a difference when there is none.

misconceptions.label: type I = missing an effect
misconceptions.description: A type I error is concluding no difference when there is one.

title: Type II error
definition: Type II errors refer to failing to reject a wrong null hypothesis: concluding that no difference exists when there is one.
intro: Missing a difference that is there.

constraints.text: Type II error: failing to reject a false null hypothesis, concluding no difference when one exists.

misconceptions.label: type II = false alarm
misconceptions.description: A type II error is concluding there is a difference when there is none.

title: Power
definition: Beta is the probability of making a type II error and power is 1 - beta; increasing the sample size, improving the precision of the measurement and increasing the expected effect size increase power (and decrease beta).
intro: How likely a study is to find a difference that is really there.

constraints.text: Beta = P(type II error); power = 1 - beta; increasing the sample size, measurement precision or expected effect size increases power and decreases beta.

misconceptions.label: fewer subjects, more power
misconceptions.description: Excluding participants reduces the chance of a type II error.

title: The p-value
definition: A p-value below 0.05 means that, if there were truly no difference (the null hypothesis), a result at least this extreme would occur less than 5% of the time; 0.05 is the usual threshold. A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05.
intro: The usual line for 'statistically significant'.

constraints.text: p < 0.05 means a result at least this extreme would occur less than 5% of the time if the null hypothesis were true ('unlikely to be due to chance alone'), i.e. statistically significant at the usual threshold.
A 95% confidence interval that does not contain 1 (for a ratio) corresponds to p < 0.05; one that contains 1 to p > 0.05.

misconceptions.label: p measures effect size
misconceptions.description: A smaller p-value means a larger, more important effect.

misconceptions.label: p and CI unrelated
misconceptions.description: A 95% CI that excludes 1 can still have p = 0.5.

title: Confidence intervals
definition: The confidence interval represents an interval where the true value most likely falls (a 95% chance for a 95% CI). For results to be statistically significant it must not contain the value 1, and the entire interval must fall on the same side of 1.
intro: Read the interval against the null value: 1 for ratios, 0 for differences.

constraints.text: A 95% confidence interval is the range of plausible values for the true value: intervals built this way contain it 95% of the time.
For RR or OR the result is statistically significant only if the interval does not contain 1.
The entire interval must be on one side of 1: above 1 = risk factor, below 1 = protective.
For a difference (e.g. blood pressure change) the null value is 0.

misconceptions.label: any interval reaching above 1 is a risk
misconceptions.description: An RR interval of 0.1-3.6 shows a significant risk because it reaches 3.6.

misconceptions.label: 95% chance the point estimate is exact
misconceptions.description: A 95% CI means a 95% chance the point estimate is exactly right.

title: Clinical significance
definition: A statistically significant result can still be unlikely to lead to clinically improved outcomes, e.g. a blood pressure decrease of 2.3 mmHg or fasting glucose falling from 135.5 to 133.9.
intro: Significant is not the same as important.

constraints.text: Clinical significance asks whether a difference is large enough to improve outcomes, which statistical significance does not tell you.
A significant drop from 135.5 to 133.9 mg/dL (or 2.3 mmHg) is unlikely to be clinically significant.

misconceptions.label: significant = important
misconceptions.description: Any statistically significant result is clinically important.

title: t-test
definition: t-test is used to compare the means of two groups.
intro: Two groups, one average each: are they different?

constraints.text: A t-test compares the means of two groups.

misconceptions.label: t-test for many groups
misconceptions.description: Use a t-test to compare the means of five groups.

title: ANOVA
definition: ANOVA test is done to compare the means of 3 or more groups.
intro: Three or more groups, one average each.

constraints.text: ANOVA compares the means of three or more groups.

misconceptions.label: ANOVA for proportions
misconceptions.description: Use ANOVA to compare the percentage of smokers in three age groups.

title: Chi-square test
definition: Chi-square test is used to compare the differences between 2 or more percentages or proportions of categorical outcomes. It is not used to compare mean values.
intro: Percentages, not averages.

constraints.text: Chi-square compares percentages or proportions of categorical outcomes, not means.
Fisher's exact test checks differences between 2 percentages or proportions of categorical outcomes.

misconceptions.label: chi-square for means
misconceptions.description: Use chi-square to compare mean blood pressure between states.
